## `=/2` inline again, and a loop slowed by where its code sits (1.13.5)

cicili-lang reported its loop of three `=/2`s a turn
(`eq(N) :- X = f(N, a), X = f(_, Y), Y = a, N1 is N - 1, eq(N1).`) at
1.460 s for ten million turns on 1.12.1, 1.592 s on 1.12.2 and 1.706 s on
1.13.0. Built here from the three commits and counted beside 1.13.4
(callgrind, a hundred thousand turns, work less padding as
`tools/flow/zero.sh` counts it): 2 321.6 instructions a turn on 1.12.1,
2 335.0 on 1.12.2, 2 335.1 on 1.13.0, 2 336.4 on 1.13.4.

* **1.12.2's 13 instructions were the call.** `coco_bi_unify` was one line
  through 1.12.1, and clang inlined it into the builtin switch by itself
  (no instruction of it in the profile; 24 a turn in `coco_builtin_call`).
  The count of `frees` made it a call: 39 a turn in `coco_bi_unify` and 24
  fewer in the switch. It is `(static) (inline)` now, always inlined: 2 324.4
  a turn, 1.12.1's and the three increments of `frees`, which are the two
  clocks' price. nrev, queens and lookup count the same to the instruction.
* **1.13.0's time was not in the instructions.** Ten alternating rounds of
  three million turns: 1.12.1 0.611 s (median), 1.12.2 0.623, 1.13.0 0.673,
  1.13.4 0.667 -- 8 % at 1.13.0 for the same instructions. 1.13.0 added
  about 700 lines of functions, and everything after them moved:
  `coco_clause_run`, a quarter of the loop's instructions, began on a
  64-byte line through 1.12.2 and 32 bytes into one since. Built with
  every function on a 64-byte line (`-falign-functions=64`), the loop's best
  time was 1.12.2's again (0.574 s against 0.577) -- but over the five bench
  tasks and the loop together, eight rounds, the flag moved nothing past
  this box's noise (loop -4 %, nrev, queens, lookup and sortnums within
  2 %), and on this box 1.13.5 is as fast as 1.12.2 or faster on all five
  (loop -10 %, queens -5 %), so it was not adopted: a placement that helps
  one loop is another's lottery. Inlining `=/2` buys no time this box can
  see (its rounds are within the noise); it is shipped for the count, the
  path 1.12.1 had.

## The two shifts take any count (1.14.0)

cicilang's report: `X is 1 >> 64` answered 1, `1 << 1000000` answered 1,
`-256 >> 66` answered -64, and `1 >> -1` answered what `1 >> 63` does. In C
a shift by a count of 64 or more, or by a negative count, is UNDEFINED
(C11 6.5.7/3); x86-64 and aarch64 both take the count modulo 64, which is
why the answer was the same wrong answer on either machine and why no
error was raised. They found it where a quad long double written as its
low 64 bits and its high bits did not move, and their own constant folder
had the fault too; a mask built as `(1 << 64) - 1` came out 0 and a store
through it wrote nothing.

Both evaluators -- `coco_arith` in lib/solve.cicili and the guards' runner,
written once in lib/kb.cicili and emitted three times -- now call
`coco_shift_right` and `coco_shift_left` (lib/term.cicili, static, the four
callers' own). The answers are SWI's, as far as a 61-bit integer carries
them:

* a count past 63 gives `>>` the sign of its left side, 0 or -1, where an
  arithmetic shift ends and what SWI's unbounded integers answer;
* a count past 63 gives `<<` 0, which is what the 61 bits a cell keeps
  already made of `1 << 61` (SWI, with no width, answers 2^61);
* a negative count shifts the other way, as SWI's does -- `1 >> -1` is 2,
  `8 >> -2` is 32, `4 << -1` is 2 -- and a magnitude past 63 is the other
  direction's rule, tested BEFORE the negation that the smallest integer
  would overflow;
* the left shift goes through u64, because a left shift of a negative
  value is undefined as well (6.5.7/4) and the bit pattern two's
  complement wants is the one an unsigned shift leaves.

WHAT IT COSTS, against 1.13.7 (`sh tools/flow/zero.sh`, work less
padding): nrev +1 780 instructions in all (+0.0027 %), queens +15 496
(+0.037 %), lookup +22 504 (+0.047 %). None of the three shifts at all,
so the cost is not the two helpers running: it is the branches they put
in the guards' AG_BIN switch, which moved the runner's registers --
lookup's bodies start with arithmetic (`V is (K * 7) mod 1000`), so every
clause it enters runs that switch. A build with both helpers
`(static) (inline)` -- which takes no `(decl)`, Cicili refusing an inline
function declared and defined apart -- counted within 200 instructions of
this one on all three, so clang was already inlining them and the forced
form was not kept.

A count of 0 to 63 is unmoved, which is every count any case asked for
before. `test/engine.pl`'s `shifts` section holds all three paths that
evaluate arithmetic -- the step, a guard at clause entry, a goal done in
place from an environment -- to a table of 34 rows, each row swipl 9.0.4's
own answer except the two the 61 bits cut short. THE ARM is the 1.13.6
binary: 20 of the 34 rows wrong on each of the three paths. `test/errors.pl`,
`test/gc.pl`, `test/window.pl` and `test/meter.pl` are green with it.

Recorded while writing the section, and left for 1.15.0 (below, where it
is fixed): a shift by a float raised `type_error(integer, P)` whose culprit
P was the loaded file's path, not the float (`coco_type_error` was given
cell 0, which is a real heap cell). Older than this change; `sh_shape/2`
held the error's shape without its culprit so that a fix would find a
check to tighten, and 1.15.0 tightened it.

## The whole run's time by predicate, where the largest call is, and what is not an integer named (1.15.0)

A minor, the owner's: a program can reach something new --
`'$trace_window'/4`'s `run_time(R)`, library(flow/debug)'s
`flow_run_time/3` and `flow_run_time_text/2`, and `tools/flow/debug.pl`'s
`profile=run`. There are three parts. The first two are cicilang's two
wishes for the time view, and the third is the culprit 1.14.0 recorded.

**What is not an integer is named by its value.** Every function that
takes integers alone (`//`, div, mod, rem, gcd, `>>`, `<<`, the bitwise
four and msb) raised `type_error(integer, P)` with P set to heap cell 0,
whatever the machine had put there first. Under `-s` that was the loaded
file's path; under `cocolog run FILE G` it was G's own name. They now
name the float through `coco_not_integer`, as swipl 9.0.4 does:

* the left operand when both are floats;
* the value an expression came to, not the expression
  (`(1.0 + 0.5) >> 1` names 1.5);
* and msb/1 of an integer under 1 is
  `domain_error(not_less_than_one, N)`.

A guard that meets a float hands its goal to the step, as it always did,
and so does a goal done in place, so the step names the float on all
three paths. `test/engine.pl`'s `integers_only` section holds the three
paths to 19 rows, each swipl's own answer (its context apart). It holds
the step alone to 9 more (gcd, the complement, msb, an operand that is
an expression), and the complement of a float to its answer in a guard
and in place. `shifts` now checks the culprit as well as the error's
shape.

* THE ARM is the 1.14.0 binary. It answered every row wrong on every
  path (19, 19, 19 and 9) and both complements wrong, each with
  `type_error(integer, integers_only)` when run as
  `cocolog run test/engine.pl integers_only`.

**Where a predicate's largest call is, and a load counted from the
outside** (wish 2). Each row of the time view carries
`at(From-To, Step)`, written ` @W:S`. That is the window, and the step
its largest call was made at: the earliest of any call that took that
long, read from the call event's own step. A window of a few thousand
steps recorded around S then reads that call with its arguments. Two
windows added up keep the position of the one that held the call; the
case cuts a run five steps before msort/2's call and finds it at `@2:S`.

The load mark, `(one call: P %)`, wants the largest call to be ten times
the mean of the others. Through 1.14.0 it counted every call, so a
recursion called twice alike was marked: the 2 000 calls inside the
first call were "the others", and their mean was nearly nothing. Lesson
51's `count/1` read `(one call: 51.9 %)`. The rule now counts a
predicate's OUTERMOST calls, those no call of it in the window is above,
as `outer(N, Ns)` on the row, which merged windows add up. The CALL TREE
names those calls, not the spans. A recursion redone for its next answer
makes its inner calls after its first Exit, where its span has ended, so
the spans counted every one of the 31 calls of `nat(X), X >= 30`
outermost.

* ARM A, 1.14.0's rule over every call, is red on two checks: t_r/1 is
  marked, and the outermost counts are every call
  (`t_c/1-201, t_r/1-4002`).
* ARM B, outermost by span, is red on one: t_nat/1 counts 31.

The load fixture had been flaky since 1.13.7, and that was the fixture's
fault, not the rule's. t_e/1 made a list of 300, some 25 us, with its
first call about three times its second (a first call's own cost). A
single stall of 50 us made the ten times that marks a load, once in a
run of the case. t_e/1 makes 3 000 now and t_r/1 recurses 2 000. Over
eight runs, the larger call of each pair was between 1.3 and 2.9 times
the other.

**The whole run's self time by predicate, at every step** (wish 1:
"self time alone, by predicate over the whole run, would serve us well";
the windows had covered 0.7 % of a run). The clock is `time(1, 0)`'s,
read at every step from the first, with no window, no replay and no
chart. Each reading charges the time since the last to the KEY of the
step that ran: 1 + (a functor's id << 1), 1 + (an atom's id << 1 | 1),
or 0 for a step that hands back a solution. The keys index an array that
doubles as keys arrive (`kns`, `kst` on the recorder).

`coco_clock_key` reads the key at the step's top, from what the loop is
about to take, and changes nothing: the registers' `afid`, `ngoal`, a
`'$k'` frame's goal, or an environment unit's `fid` or its slot's term.
A retry is charged to the predicate retried. It is read from the key of
the step it ran in (`rpk`) and moved to the predicate's index in the
store (`rpp`), which is named once as the run ends. A collection is kept
apart (`GcNs`, `Gcs`), as in the window's clock. `flow_run_time/3` takes
the clock's own cost off each row: about 30 ns a reading on this box.
The clock calibrates that cost as it is armed, as `time(F, K)`'s does,
and hands it over as `run_time/7`'s N and ClockNs.

* **A nested engine is asked its goal BEFORE it is narrowed**, at
  findall/3, call_limited/3 and with_output_to/2. The narrow is where the
  clock names the new engine's first goal, and an ask leaves the limits
  alone. The starter's own key is kept on the starter (`e->tkey`, not
  `kcall`, which a collection may have made stale) and given back in
  `coco_clock_back`, so findall/3's copying stays findall/3's.
* **A guard a clause runs as it is entered is no step the clock reads.**
  Its time belongs to its clause's predicate, so is/2 run that way has no
  row. A control construct is a row of its own.
* `run_time(R)` is refused beside `time(F, K)` and with `from(I)`.
  `profile=run` is asked by name: it is not part of `all`, and `all,run`
  asks for both.

THE ARMS are engine builds, each red on its own checks in
`test/window.pl`'s `run_timed` section and green on the rest:

* ARM R leaves a retry's time on the key of the step it ran in. It is
  red on 3: the retry check (w_pk/1's 200 retries), findall/3's inner
  steps, and its copies.
* ARM N narrows before the ask, as through 1.14.0. It is red on 2: the
  first inner step is not its goal's, and the copies.
* ARM B gives no key back in `coco_clock_back`. It is red on 2:
  findall/3's copies are charged to its last inner goal, and so is each
  answer's copy as it is made.

`test/flowdebug.pl`'s `run_timed` section holds library(flow/debug)'s
rows: who has them, with how many steps, in which order, a retry's
time, the text, and the shell's `profile=time,run`. Lesson 51 shows the
whole run with msort/2 on top and count/1's 402 steps with no is/2 row.

**WHAT IT COSTS.** A run that asks for neither clock pays what it did.
`sh tools/flow/zero.sh`, 1.14.0 against 1.15.0, work less padding:

| | 1.14.0 | 1.15.0 | instructions |
|---|---|---|---|
| nrev | 66 583 490 | 66 583 461 | -29 |
| queens | 41 657 938 | 41 657 956 | +18 |
| lookup | 47 425 449 | 47 425 451 | +2 |

A run that asks for the clock costs about twice its time. Three probes

| `time(1, 0)` | 274 to 330 |

## Integers of 64 bits, and text in characters by default (2.0.0)

A major, the owner's number: programs that worked can stop. Two changes
are in it, by the owner's choice: integers of 64 bits, loud past them,
and characters as the default text unit.

### Integers are 64 bits, and say so past them

Through 1.15.0 an integer was a cell's 61 bits, and a result past them
WRAPPED in silence: `1000000000000000000 * 997` was 875820019684212736.
COMPAT.md's silent table led with it. Now:

* **A value past 61 bits is BOXED.** A BIG cell (tag 7) indexes the
  machine's `bigs`, an array of i64, as a FLT cell indexes its floats.
  It is canonical by range: a value that fits a cell is always an INT
  cell, so an INT never equals a BIG, and two INT cells still compare
  by word.
* **Past 64 bits arithmetic raises `evaluation_error(int_overflow)`**
  where SWI makes a bignum. That holds for `+`, `-`, `*`, `**`, `^`, the
  least integer `//` or `div` -1, its `-` and `abs`, a `<<` that loses a
  bit, succ/2, plus/3, sum_list/2 and numlist/3. It also holds for a float
  made an integer outside the range; an infinity or a NaN is
  `evaluation_error(undefined)`.
* **The reader counts in u64.** A literal past 2^63-1 (2^63 for a
  negative one) is `integer out of range`.
* **Two integers are ordered exactly.** Through 1.15.0
  `9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992` was true, both compared as
  doubles. An integer and a float still compare as doubles, the float
  first when equal, as swipl 9.0.4 has it.
* **The flags:** `bounded` is `true`, `max_integer` and `min_integer`
  are ±2^63, `max_tagged_integer` and `min_tagged_integer` the cell's.

The overflow test is `__builtin_add_overflow` and its two kin (`coco_add_ovf`,
`_sub_`, `_mul_`): an add or an imul and a `jo`. The first build tested in
128 bits, which made an add nine instructions (sar, adc), and lookup counted
1.5 % more (76 810 626 instructions against 1.15.0's 75 702 867, callgrind).
The builtins, the guards' stops and GUARDX on cells brought it to the
+0.38 % of work below.

Two places took a different road:

* **The guards stop where they cannot decide**, as they always did for a
  float. GUARDX computes on the cells themselves (A+B is CA-2+CB), where
  a 64-bit overflow is exactly a result past the cell's 61 bits.
* **`cc_match_const` asks the word first**, so a clause head's integer
  costs the match nothing new.

The tables reclaim `bigs` with the floats and strings. A frozen machine
carries them in a `B` section. The index keys a BIG as it keys a float, as
0. `test/engine.pl`'s `integers_64` section (145 checks) holds the step, a
guard and a goal in place to swipl 9.0.4's answers. Twelve arms take one
rule out each and go red:

| arm | red |
|---|---|
| the step's overflow test (two builds) | 5 and 5 |
| the guards' overflow tests (two) | 3 and 1 |
| the guards' fit to a cell | 6 |
| GUARDX's overflow test (two) | 4 and 4 |
| the tables' marking of `bigs` | 19 |
| the index key of a BIG | 1 |
| the exact order | 1 |
| unify by value | 2 |
| the freeze's `B` section | 1 |

`tools/flow/zero.sh` against 1.15.0, counting work less the padding:

| | instructions |
|---|---|
| nrev | -0.16 % |
| queens | +0.26 % |
| lookup | +0.38 % |

The time pairs were within the box's noise.

The linter lost rule A1, which flagged an integer literal past 61 bits.
The card lost rows A2 and O1, the literal and the order: the divergences
they named are gone. `test/bigint.pl` pinned the wrong answer as its
reason; it pins the error now.

Not SWI's, and staying so:

* past 64 bits cocolog raises where swipl goes on in a bignum;
* `2**63 - 1` raises, its `2**63` coming first;
* atom_number/2 and number_codes/2 fail for a numeral past 64 bits.

### Rationals, and the rest of swipl's arithmetic and text (2.5.0)

A rational is a numerator and a denominator, each 64 bits, reduced with a
positive denominator and never with 1 (that is an integer). A result past
them raises `evaluation_error(int_overflow)` where swipl makes a bignum --
`X is 1r2 ** 100`, `X is rational(1.0e308)`, `lcm(9223372036854775807, 2)`
-- `rational(1.0Inf)` is `rational_overflow`, `rational(1.5NaN)` and
`rationalize(1.5NaN)` `undefined`, and a value whose exact fraction does not
fit (a subnormal) is int_overflow too. The reader takes `N r D` as one
token; `1r0` is `syntax_error(illegal_number)`.

**A rational has a tag of its own, and that moved every cell.** Since 2.5.0
the tag field is four bits and the payload 60: RAT is tag 8, so a rational
is no longer a BIG cell with bit 63 set, an INT holds -2^59 .. 2^59-1
inline (2^59 and past are boxed), and `max_tagged_integer` is 2^59-1. A
frozen machine's header is `cocolog 2`; a format-1 blob (every build through
2.4.1) is upgraded as it thaws (`coco_thaw_upgrade`): the old tags are
re-encoded, a BIG that set bit 63 was a rational, and an INT that no longer
fits is boxed after the `B` and `R` sections are read, so every old index
still names what it named. Proved against two machines frozen by the 2.4.1
binary -- one at `start`, one stepped three times -- holding 2^59,
-2^59-1, `5r6` and a small integer; both resumed under the new binary to
the same answer (`576460752303423488/-576460752303423489/5r6/12345/
576460752303423489/7r6`).

**The suite's wait helper is a wall clock** (2.5.0): `proc_until/3` used to
count only its own sleeps, so `unix_listening/1` -- whose `lsof` prints no
unix-socket state on macOS -- spent each try's own time on top and took
about 26 s against its stated eight, outlasting the ten-second accepts in
the tcp, websocket and curl fixtures. It now ends at the budget with
`get_time/1`; the tcp fixture's first accept waits a minute for margin.
**The suite loads `library/*.so` and does not build them**: a stale
`library/tcp.so` that predated the `unix(Path)` source failed tcp, httpd,
websocket and curl in one run. `make modules` before the suite.

Not SWI's, and staying so:

* the random generator is xoshiro128**, not Mersenne Twister: the API is
  swipl's, the sequence is not, and `random_property(state(S))` answers
  `'$rng_state'(A,B,C,D)`, four hex atoms. `set_random(seed(N))` repeats
  within cocolog and not across systems;
* swipl 10's `cmpr/2`, `maxr/2` and `minr/2` are absent (the reference is
  9.0.4), and so are `random_between/3` and the rest of `library(random)`,
  `library(strings)` and the stream string predicates (`read_string/3,5`,
  `open_string/2`).

The measured cost, five alternating pairs of user time against the
released 2.4.1 binary (the Mac, release, one sitting; nrev `main(1000,50)`,
queens `main(8,500)`, lookup `main(2000,8000)`): naive reverse +4.7 %
(1.258 s to 1.317 s), queens -0.1 %, lookup -1.3 %. A rational-only build,
measured before the four-bit tag refactor, was +4.0 % on nrev with queens
and lookup unchanged, so the refactor's own share of the +4.7 % is under
the noise of one pair. The new code before `lib/kb.cicili`'s clause runners
moved them by some 3.5 KB, and the owner's record already has a 32-byte
move costing 8 % -- so the figure is the price of the code's PLACEMENT as
much as of its tests. The machine's own new fields were appended on that
account, though appending changed nothing measurable.

### Text is characters by default, and the wire is bytes

`text_units` (1.13.0) defaults to characters, SWI's: `atom_length('dár',
N)` is 3 and `atom_codes/2` gives code points. Bytes are asked for, by
`:- set_prolog_flag(text_units, bytes).` or COCOLOG_TEXT_UNITS=bytes, and
give 1.x's answers. A frozen machine thaws in the units it was frozen in;
one frozen before 1.13.0 carries no `U` and thaws in bytes.

**The flip broke the network libraries, and they are mended.** They
turned text into wire bytes, and back, with atom_codes/2, which now
answers code points:

* library(http) decoded `caf%C3%A9` to the path `cafÃ©`, read each byte of
  a raw UTF-8 header as a character, and put a body's code points on the
  wire one byte each, with a Content-Length that counted characters;
* httpd served a binary file a byte short (`the body length is the file's
  byte count`: 62 of 63);
* library(websocket) refused to send `héllo`: its code points went to
  the UTF-8 check as bytes.

The new builtin is SWI's `string_bytes(?Text, ?Bytes, utf8)`: a text's
UTF-8 bytes, or the string some bytes make, the same in both units. The
libraries cross at the wire with it. A socket stays bytes (library(tcp),
library(tls), a binary or a ping message). What the program is handed,
and what it hands over, is text in its units: the atoms, a request's body,
a text message, a curl response.

**curl's bytes past 127 came back NEGATIVE, in either unit**: `café` was
`[99,97,102,-61,-87]`. Its buffer is `char *`, signed here, and each byte
was widened as it stood. That is older than both changes and found by
them. The body is built with `coco_m_codes_of` now.

library(flow) counted a code of 128..191 as a continuation byte. Its
widths and columns ask the flag past 127 now: under characters such a
code is a character of its own (a `»`, a no-break space).

Cases and lessons that pinned bytes were moved to the default:

* a byte witness reads bytes through string_bytes/3 (stream, ray,
  serialize);
* a check of bytes behaviour runs a child under bytes (errors' 1.11.8
  crash, stream's put_code/get_code, units, translate's
  `newspaper_units`, which names both units now);
* lessons basics/08 and 13, library 12, 37 and 48 teach characters, and
  lesson 13 reads and runs a part of itself in bytes.

New checks, each red with 1.15.0's library or module and green under both
units:

| where | checks |
|---|---|
| `test/http.pl`, `text past ASCII` | 8 |
| `test/curl.pl` (1.15.0's module) | 3 |
| `test/websocket.pl` (the session ends at `ws_send`) | 1 |
| `test/units.pl`, string_bytes/3 against swipl | 10 |

The translator's case takes 30 s, as it did under bytes at the 1.15.0
gate. The reasoning library reads both units since 1.13.2, and its byte
clauses can go, on its own number.

## =@=/2, \=@=/2 and subsumes_term/2, and term_variables/2 linear (2.1.0)

Through 2.0.0 a call of `=@=/2` or `subsumes_term/2` was an existence
error, and `a =@= b` was a syntax error. Now they are SWI's, with
`\=@=/2` beside them, and `=@=` and `\=@=` are operators at 700 xfx.

* **subsumes_term(General, Specific)** collects Specific's variables, then
  unifies the two. It asks whether each variable is still unbound and no
  two were made one, then undoes the unify, so it binds nothing. SWI binds
  each variable to `[]` and asks the next; here each goes into the
  borrowed variable map. A variable the two share is Specific's, so
  `subsumes_term(f(A, b), f(a, A))` is no.
* **A =@= B** copies A first, a fresh variable for each of its own, and
  asks whether the copy and B each subsume the other. Two terms with no
  variable in common are variants exactly when that holds. Asked as they
  stand, `x(A, B) =@= x(B, A)` would bind A and B together on the first
  unify and answer no, where SWI says yes. Nothing points into the copy
  once both questions are undone, so the heap is set back to where it was.
* **Every walk under them is one of the cycle-safe ones** (term_variables/2's
  collector, unify, copy_term/2's copy), so a cycle, a DAG that doubles at
  each of 40 levels, and a list of 200 000 variables all finish, with
  swipl's answers.

**term_variables/2 was quadratic in the variables it found.** It looked
each one up by scanning the ones it had. 200 000 distinct variables took
6.8 s, where swipl takes 0.07, and the two new builtins walk Specific's
variables the same way: 7.1 s and 14.4 s. Past sixteen variables it now
asks the variable map, which holds them all by then. The same 200 000
take 0.027 s, subsumes_term/2 over them 0.053 s and =@=/2 0.16 s. Up to
sixteen the scan is unchanged.

`test/files/variant.pl` is run by swipl 9.0.4 and by cocolog, and its 82
lines agree byte for byte:

* SWI's and ISO's examples, shared variables, and `'$VAR'` terms;
* cycles, the DAG, the long list, and 64-bit integers;
* nothing left bound afterwards;
* the operators as the reader, the writer and current_op/3 see them.

`test/engine.pl` adds a section of three checks, each a child under a
timeout:

* 400 000 variables are found in their order inside six seconds;
* subsumes_term/2 and =@=/2 over 200 000 finish inside eight;
* =@=/2 leaves no copy on the heap.

Nine arms take one rule out each, and each goes red:

| arm | red |
|---|---|
| Specific's variables still unbound | 16 lines of the 82 |
| no two of them made one | 10 lines |
| the unify undone | 7 lines |
| the copy before =@=/2 asks | 8 lines |
| asked both ways | 4 lines |
| the copy taken back off the heap | 1 check (640 072 bytes left) |
| the variable map past sixteen | 2 checks (timed out) |
| the two operators | the file does not read; 2 checks |
| their lines in library/flow/modes.pl | 1 check of `test/flowchart.pl` |

**Still not SWI's:** `0.0 =@= -0.0` holds, as `0.0 = -0.0` and
`0.0 == -0.0` do. cocolog's unify and compare take the two zeros as equal
and a NaN as unequal to itself, where SWI tells floats apart by their
bits. COMPAT.md has the row; =@=/2 inherits it from unify.

## Floats are told apart by their bits (2.1.1)

The owner's choice after 2.1.0. Through 2.1.0 two floats were compared as
numbers wherever a term was:

* `0.0 = -0.0`, `0.0 == -0.0` and `0.0 =@= -0.0` held;
* `p(0.0)` answered the goal `p(-0.0)`, and a first-argument index over
  `k(0.0, _)` and `k(-0.0, _)` handed back both;
* `sort/2` kept one of the two zeros;
* no NaN unified, not even with itself;
* a NaN, equal to every number in the order, left a sort OUT OF ORDER:
  `msort([2, NaN, 1.0, -1, NaN])` came back as `[NaN, 1.0, NaN, -1, 2]`.

Now they are swipl 9.0.4's:

* **Two float cells are one term when their bits are** (`coco_flt_eq`). It
  is asked by unify (`coco_unify` and its linked walk), by the store's
  matcher (both of its arms), and by a compiled head's constant.
* **Two floats that do not order as numbers** (`coco_flt_order`, asked by
  `coco_num_order`) put a NaN before any other number. Two zeros, or two
  NaNs, go by their bits taken as a signed integer, so `-0.0 @< 0.0`. An
  integer against a float is as before: as doubles, the float first when
  they are equal, so `-0.0 @< 0.0 @< 0`.

Arithmetic still compares numbers (`0.0 =:= -0.0`). Over a NaN, and in
`max`/`min` of the two zeros, it is not SWI's yet: COMPAT.md has the row.
(2.1.2 made both SWI's, below.)

`test/files/float_order.pl` is run by swipl and by cocolog, and its 72
lines agree byte for byte. They cover unify, `==/2`, `memberchk/2`,
`unify_with_occurs_check/2`, `subsumes_term/2` and `=@=/2`; unify past its
count, over cyclic terms; the order under `compare/3`, msort/2, sort/2
and sort/4, keysort/2, setof/3 and list_to_ord_set/2; compiled heads and
their index; asserted clauses and `retract/1`; and the text and copies of
`-0.0`. 2.1.0 differs from swipl on 50 of the 72. No program reaches the
store's matcher (every clause a program can write compiles), so
`test/solve.cicili` asks it directly, with five checks.

Seven arms take one rule out each, and each goes red:

| arm | red |
|---|---|
| unify | 17 lines of the 72 |
| unify's linked walk | 2 lines (the cyclic ones) |
| the store's matcher, a store variable met again | 1 check of `test/solve.cicili` |
| the store's matcher, a stored float | 2 checks |
| a compiled head's constant | 7 lines |
| a NaN first | 8 lines |
| the two zeros by their bits | 18 lines |

`tools/flow/zero.sh` against 2.1.0, counting work less padding:

| | instructions |
|---|---|
| nrev | +0.003 % |
| queens | +0.027 % |
| lookup | +0.005 % |

## Arithmetic over a NaN, and max and min, as SWI's are (2.1.2)

The owner's choice after 2.1.1. Through 2.1.1:

* a NaN compared equal to every number: `X =:= X`, `=<` and `>=` held of
  a NaN and `=\=` failed, and `1.5NaN =:= 1.0` held;
* `max` and `min` made both floats when either was one and took the
  doubles' `<`: `max(2, 1.5)` was `2.0`, `max(0.0, -0.0)` was `-0.0`,
  `min(-0.0, 0.0)` was `0.0`, and `max(1.0, NaN)` was the NaN;
* `max_list/2` and `min_list/2` kept the first of two equal numbers
  (`max_list([1, 1.0], M)` was `1`) and stopped at a NaN;
* `aggregate_all/3`'s `sum`, `max` and `min` worked in doubles: `2^53 + 1`
  summed to `2^53`, `2^62 + (2^62 - 1)` to the least integer, and the
  larger of two integers past `2^53` was the first;
* `sign/1` of a NaN was `0.0`.

Now they are swipl 9.0.4's:

* **A NaN is unordered.** `coco_num_cmp` answers 2, so `=\=` holds and
  the other five fail.
* **`max` and `min` are SWI's `ar_max` and `ar_min`** (`coco_num_pick`,
  which answers which of the two). A NaN is passed over; -0.0 is the
  smaller zero; of an integer and a float that are equal, the float; and
  the one picked is answered as it came, so `max(2, 1.5)` is `2`.
* `max_list/2` and `min_list/2` fold `M is max(H, M0)` along the list,
  and `aggregate_all/3` folds `M is max(M0, X)`, each in the order of
  SWI's own clause (the order picks between two NaNs). The witness forms
  are `X > Max0`, with two integers compared as integers.
* `aggregate_all/3`'s sum adds integers as integers until a float
  arrives, and raises int_overflow past 64 bits, as `sum_list/2` does.
* `sign/1` of a NaN is SWI's one NaN, the bits `1.5NaN` reads as.

The guards take integers alone and never meet any of it.

Found on the way and not changed, COMPAT.md's rows: a float result that is
a NaN or infinite raises in SWI (`undefined`, `float_overflow`,
`zero_divisor`) and is the answer here; `**` and `^` with a zero exponent
or the base 1 are the integer 1 in SWI; `truncate/1` and its kin hand a
NaN or an infinity back in SWI and raise here. (All three are swipl's
since 2.2.0, below.)

`test/files/float_arith.pl` is run by swipl and by cocolog, and its 166
lines agree byte for byte. It covers:

* the six comparisons over a NaN: with literals, with variables, through
  `call/N`, `\+` and an if-then-else, in a clause whose first goal is the
  comparison, and later in a body that makes an environment;
* the zeros, the infinities, and integers past 53 bits;
* `max` and `min` in every pairing, as a guard and in an environment's
  branch;
* `sign/1`, `max_list/2` and `min_list/2`;
* `aggregate_all/3` and `aggregate/3`.

2.1.1 differs from swipl on 76 of the 166. `test/engine.pl` holds the sum
past 64 bits to int_overflow, where SWI makes a bignum.

Fifteen arms take one rule out each, and each goes red (lines of the 166
that differ from swipl):

| arm | red |
|---|---|
| a NaN equal to every number again (`coco_num_cmp`) | 27 |
| `>` true of an unordered pair | 9 |
| `>=` true of an unordered pair | 9 |
| max and min answer a float when either was one | 15 |
| a NaN not passed over | 16 |
| -0.0 not the smaller zero | 13 |
| of an integer and a float that are equal, the first | 14 |
| two integers compared as doubles | 2 (aggregate_all's, past 2^53) |
| `sign/1` of a NaN 0.0 | 3 |
| `max_list/2` and `min_list/2` as through 2.1.1 | 11 |

## A float that is no number raises, and the power is SWI's (2.2.0)

The owner's choice after 2.1.2, and the owner's number: a minor, though a
program that worked can stop (`X is 2 / 0.0` answered `1.0Inf` and raises
now). Through 2.1.2:

* a float result that was no finite number was the answer: `0.0 / 0.0` and
  `sqrt(-1.0)` a NaN, `2 / 0.0`, `10.0 ** 400` and `exp(1000)` infinities,
  `1.0Inf - 1.0Inf` a NaN;
* `**` and `^` were pow()'s float wherever a float or a negative exponent
  came in: `2.0 ** 0` and `1 ** 2.5` were `1.0`, `0 ** -1` was `1.0Inf`,
  `-1 ** -3` was `-1.0`;
* `integer/1`, `truncate/1`, `round/1`, `floor/1` and `ceiling/1` raised
  `evaluation_error(undefined)` for a NaN or an infinity;
* `log/1` refused an operand at or under zero as `undefined`.

Now they are swipl 9.0.4's, whose float flags stand at their defaults
(`float_overflow`, `float_zero_div` and `float_undefined` at `error`,
`float_underflow` at `ignore`; cocolog had no flags to change them until
2.2.2, the last section):

* **A float a function makes is a number or an error** (`coco_float_ok`,
  swipl's `check_float()`): a NaN raises `evaluation_error(undefined)`, an
  infinity `float_overflow`, and a subnormal is a number. It is asked of
  `+`, `-` and `*` (the binary macro answers 5 for a float result that is
  no finite number), `/`, `**` and `^`, `sqrt/1`, the transcendentals,
  `exp/1`, `log/1` and `float/1` (`coco_float_fn`).
* **Each float operand is checked first**, as swipl's promotion checks it:
  the dividend and the divisor of a float quotient, the base and the
  exponent of a power, the operand of a float function. So `1.0Inf / 0.0`
  is `float_overflow`, and `1.0Inf ** -1` and `sin(1.0Inf)` are
  `float_overflow` where libm answers `0.0` and a NaN.
* **`/` is swipl's `ar_divide()`**: over an infinity an integer is the
  integer `0` and a finite float a zero with the two signs' product; a
  number over a float zero is `zero_divisor`, a zero over it the NaN
  raised.
* **A power is swipl's `ar_pow()`**: `X ** 0` is the integer `1` (a NaN's
  and an infinity's too); of an integer base, `1 ** Y` is `1`, `0 ** Y` is
  `0` or a zero divisor, and `-1 ** N` is `1` or `-1` for an integer N; two
  integers under an exponent of 0 or more make the integer power; the rest
  is pow() over two checked doubles, a zero base under a negative exponent
  a zero divisor. (swipl writes the base `1.0` out as `1.0`, for libms that
  break C99; glibc's pow() answers it, so the case is not written here: an
  arm that took it out moved nothing.)
* `sum_list/2` and `aggregate_all/3`'s sum raise at the float sum that is
  no number (`coco_l_float_ok`), and **two equal infinities raise
  `float_overflow` in `max` and `min`** (`coco_num_pick` answers 2: swipl
  makes the two one type, and checks the float it makes) -- in `is/2`, in
  `max_list/2` and `min_list/2`, and in `aggregate_all/3`, whose first step
  is `M is max(X, X)`.

Unchecked, as swipl leaves them: the sign, `abs`, `-`, `+` and the
comparisons; `integer/1` and its four kin, which hand a NaN or an infinity
back as it came (`coco_float_back`); `/` over an infinity. The guards take
integers alone and never meet any of it.

`test/files/float_check.pl` is run by swipl and by cocolog, and its 194
lines agree byte for byte; 2.1.2 differs on 136 of them. `test/engine.pl`
holds `integer(1.0Inf)` and `truncate(1.5NaN)` to the float handed back.
The dialect card's A3 went with the divergence it named: it said SWI's
`2 ** 10` was `1024.0`, which is ISO's answer, where swipl 9's is the
integer `1024` as cocolog's is (lesson 37 counts 31 rows; lesson 04, the
basics README, README.md and library/llm/DESIGN.md said the same of SWI
and say what is true).

Twenty-four arms take one rule out each, and each goes red (lines of the
194 that differ from swipl):

## Not started

* Compiling a program to an object file. `DESIGN-compiling.md` is the
  feasibility report; §8's first two items are done (the collector's
  reach, widened in 1.9.6; the count of how much of a real program could
  be compiled, 1.9.4: 99.9 % of the predicates have clauses nothing changes
  by name). What follows is the owner's choice. Packaging (§8's step 3,
  §3A: a binary that carries its program and needs no `.pl` beside it) is
  something new reachable from a program, so a minor, 1.10.0, PROPOSED
  rather than taken; its first task is §10.5's, the binary's one RUNPATH
  being the build's own `$(ZIGURATIP)/home/lib` (Makefile:181), so the
  binary finds ZiguratIP's libraries only where they were when it was
  linked, or through `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. Emitting C (step 4) first needs
  the interpreter's functions reachable from an object the compiler
  writes, by one of two roads: a runtime split out of `cocolog.c` (§10.3,
  28 556 lines in one translation unit), or chosen statics exported
  through `-rdynamic` (Makefile:189: 411 `coco_*` functions are exported,
  43 of them the SDK's `coco_m_*`).
* The Coco — the intelligent aggregator hub this project's machinery makes
  possible: chains as knowledge bases, consensus as clauses, contracts
  that learn. Its missions moved to their own repository, where the hub
  is built OF cocolog programs, not INTO cocolog — Prolog modules, its
  own Parsi objects and choreography, using cicili, ZiguratIP and
  cocolog and modifying none of them. cocolog itself remains what it
  is: a Prolog with advanced knowledge-base machinery, and the stories
  above are the foundations The Coco's STATUS.md builds on.

## swipl's float flags, and `set_prolog_flag/2` a goal (2.2.2)

The owner's ask: `set_prolog_flag(float_overflow, infinity)`. Numbered as
the patch, the default, with no owner's number to hand; what it adds is
reachable from a program, so 2.3.0 is PROPOSED for it. Through 2.2.1:

* `set_prolog_flag/2` was a directive and no goal (`existence_error` as
  one), and it knew three flags, `double_quotes`, `text_units` and
  `generate_debug_info`; any other was reported (`cocolog has no flag`)
  and the load went on;
* every float was checked as swipl's defaults check it (2.2.0), with no
  flag to change that;
* `inf`, `nan` and `epsilon` were not evaluable
  (`type_error(evaluable, inf/0)`), so `between(1, inf, X)` raised;
* `-/1` turned a NaN's sign bit over, and so did the reader's `-1.5NaN`;
* `current_prolog_flag/2` answered ten flags.

Now they are swipl 9.0.4's:

* **The four float flags** live on the machine as `fflags` (1
  `float_overflow` at `infinity`, 2 `float_zero_div` at `infinity`, 4
  `float_undefined` at `nan`, 8 `float_underflow` at `error`; 0 is swipl's
  defaults). `coco_float_verdict` is swipl's `check_float()`: a NaN is
  made swipl's one NaN (the bits `1.5NaN` reads as) and stands under
  `nan`, else raises `undefined`; an infinity stands under `infinity`,
  else raises `float_overflow`; and under `error` a subnormal raises
  `float_underflow`. `coco_zero_div` is `check_zero_div()`: a number over
  a zero is, under `infinity`, the infinity of the sign swipl gives it --
  an integer dividend's sign, of two floats the product of their signs, a
  zero base under a negative exponent `1.0Inf` but for `-0.0` under an odd
  INTEGER one (`-0.0 ** -3` is `-1.0Inf`, `-0.0 ** -3.0` `1.0Inf`) -- and
  `0 / 0` is the NaN under `float_undefined` at `nan` and a zero divisor
  under anything else, where `0.0 / 0.0` is `undefined`.
* **Where swipl checks, this checks**: every float result of `+`, `-` and
  `*` (so `float_underflow` sees a subnormal one), the float operands and
  the result of `/`, `**`, `^` and the functions, and of `max` and `min`
  over two equal floats the one picked; `sum_list/2`, `max_list/2`,
  `min_list/2` and `aggregate_all/3` ask the same verdict
  (`coco_l_float_ok`). The constants, the literals, `abs`, `sign`, `+/1`
  and `-/1` are not checked, and `integer/1` and its kin still hand a NaN
  or an infinity back.
* **`set_prolog_flag/2` is a goal** (`lb_set_flag`), raising swipl's
  errors in swipl's order. The flag comes first: `instantiation_error`,
  `type_error(atom, F)`, `existence_error(prolog_flag, F)` for a flag this
  has not got, `permission_error(modify, flag, F)` for a read-only one
  (`argv`, `os_argv`, `executable`, `bounded`, the integer and the float
  bounds). Then the value: `instantiation_error`, `type_error(atom, V)`,
  `domain_error(flag_value, V)` for a float flag,
  `domain_error(double_quotes, V)`, `domain_error(text_units, V)`, and
  `type_error(bool, V)` for `generate_debug_info`.
* **The directive keeps the reader's three** -- `double_quotes`,
  `text_units`, `generate_debug_info`, which say how the rest of the file
  is read -- and calls any other as a goal, whose refusal is reported in
  swipl's words while the load goes on.
* **A thread and `run_isolated/2` made after a set start with it**: the
  set writes the process's default too (`coco_fflags_default_set`), as
  `text_units` does. **A frozen machine keeps its flags**, in a section `N`
  after `B` (`F` is the functors'); a blob with none thaws at swipl's
  defaults.
* **`current_prolog_flag/2` answers seventeen**: the four, and
  `float_min`, `float_max` and `float_max_integer` as well.
* **`inf`, `nan` and `epsilon` are evaluable** (`*arith-names*`), and
  `between(1, inf, X)` counts for ever as swipl's does.
* **`-/1` keeps a NaN's bits**, as swipl's `ar_u_minus()` does, and the
  reader's `-1.5NaN` is `1.5NaN`.

Not swipl's yet (COMPAT.md): there is no `float_rounding`; an unknown flag
raises `existence_error` where swipl makes it (`user_flags` is `silent`);
`argv` and `os_argv` are read-only; a flag a thread sets becomes the
process's default, where swipl keeps it the thread's; and
`between(1, infinite, X)` raises.

`test/files/float_flags.pl` is run by swipl and by cocolog, and its 925

expressions under six settings (the defaults, each flag alone, all four
together), each setting's flags read back first. 2.2.1 differs on 788 of

sets a flag, and the load going on past two refused ones, each reported
in swipl's words; a thread made after a goal set it; and a machine frozen

## A prefix operator before a number, as swipl writes it (2.2.3)

The owner's ask: `+(1)`. Through 2.2.2 the writer put a space between every
symbolic prefix operator and a digit after it -- `+ 1`, `+ 1.0Inf`, `\ 1`,
`\+ 1`, `?- 1`, `:- 1`, `f(+ 1)`, `1- + 1` -- where swipl 9 writes `+1`,
`+1.0Inf`, `\1`, `\+1`, `?-1`, `:-1`, `f(+1)` and `1- +1`. The rule was
written for `-`, whose `-1` reads back as the integer and not as `-(1)`, and
it was applied to every symbolic operator, though `+1` and `\1` read back as
the operator applied to 1 in both systems. Now the digit's space is `-`'s
alone (the writer's prefix branch in `lib/syntax.cicili`). What stays: a
symbol character after the operator takes a space by the merge rule (`- -1`,
`+ -1`, `+ +1`, `\ +1`), an opening parenthesis takes one (`- (1+2)`,
`+ (+)`), and an alphabetic operator always takes one (`dynamic 1`).

`test/files/prefix_write.pl` writes 60 terms with `write/1` and `writeq/1`
and reads each back with term_to_atom/2, and swipl and cocolog agree byte for
byte; 2.2.2 differs on 26 of the lines. `test/syntax.cicili` has eleven
golden trips and six round trips more: with the old rule nine of the trips go
red, and the two others pin the spaces the merge rule keeps (`+ -1`,
`+ - 1`). Left as they were, and in COMPAT.md: write_canonical/1 keeps
operators (the dialect card's W1); `print/1` writes as `write/1` does,
unquoted, where swipl's quotes (`print('a b')` is `a b`, a row of its own
now); and `"1"` is a code list here.

library, reconsult, script and repl, and the card check. flowdebug was red

is marked) and green alone. `make test` has not been run on it.

## print/1 and `~p`, swipl's (2.2.4)

The owner's ask, after 2.2.3: print/1 too. Through 2.2.3 print/1 was
write/1 (the engine's row named `coco_bi_write`, and a clause
`print(X) :- write(X).` under it that the row shadowed) and format's `~p`
was `~w`, so `print('a b')` wrote `a b`, `print(f('X'))` `f(X)`, and
neither read back as what it printed; library(stream)'s print/2, which is
`format(S, '~p', [T])`, the same. swipl's print/1 is
`write_term(T, [portray(true), numbervars(true), quoted(true)])`, and its
`~p` calls it.

Now print/1, `~p` and so print/2 write quoted, with numbervars
(`coco_write_print`): a fourth bit in the writer's mode word, 8, carried to
every argument with quoted and ignore_ops (`mode & 11`, where it was
`mode & 3`), asked of each compound of arity 1 named `$VAR` before
anything else (`coco_write_numbervar`), and taken by the top of the write
and the cyclic writer, which take the mode word whole where they took two
flags. swipl's rules, measured: an integer N of 0 or more is the letter
N mod 26 and, past 25, N // 26 after it (`A`, `Z`, `A1`, `B1`,
`H354745078340568300`); a negative one `S_` and its magnitude (`S_1`), the
least integer `S_-9223372036854775808`, which is swipl's own text -- its
negation wraps; here it goes through u64 and C has no overflow; an atom
that reads as a variable (A-Z or `_`, then letters, digits and `_`) itself,
unquoted (`Foo`, `X1_y`, `_`); anything else the compound it is
(`'$VAR'(x)`, `'$VAR'('Foo bar')`, `'$VAR'("Foo")`, `'$VAR'(1.5)`,
`'$VAR'(1, 2)`). The dead clause is gone.

`test/files/print.pl` prints 81 terms with print/1, `~p`, and print/1
inside with_output_to/2 (its length), then a cyclic term holding a `$VAR`
(`@(S_1,[S_1=f(S_1,B,'a b')])`), a cyclic list and a string: 85 lines,
byte for byte with swipl; 2.2.3 differs on 58. `test/stream.pl` pins
print/2 into a stream: `['A b',B]`. Left out of the swipl file, and in
COMPAT.md: a portray/1 hook, which print/1 does not call here; write/1 and
writeq/1, which have no numbervars here (`writeq('$VAR'(1))` is
`'$VAR'(1)`, swipl's `B`); and an atom with a quote in it, written
`'don''t'` here and `'don\'t'` by swipl (both read back).

## write/1 and writeq/1, swipl's (2.2.5)

The owner's ask, after 2.2.4: writeq/1 and write/1 too. Through 2.2.4
only print/1 and `~p` took numbervars, so `write('$VAR'(1))` wrote
`$VAR(1)` and `writeq('$VAR'('Foo'))` `'$VAR'('Foo')`, where swipl writes
`B` and `Foo`; and every quoted write doubled a quote inside an atom,
`'don''t'`, where swipl's writeq/1 writes `'don\'t'` -- both read back as
the same atom -- and wrote `\a` `\b` `\v` `\f` (and `\r` in a string) as
the raw characters, where swipl writes the letters. A probe of swipl 9.0.4
first, over write/1, writeq/1, print/1, write_canonical/1, `~w` `~q` `~p`,
writeln/1, write_term/2 and term_to_atom/2, before anything was changed.

NUMBERVARS, swipl's: write/1, writeln/1, writeq/1, `~w`, `~q` (so
library(stream)'s write/2 and writeq/2, which are `~w` and `~q`), and
write_term/2's `numbervars(true)`, which was read past (2.2.4's rules for
what `'$VAR'(N)` becomes, unchanged); write_canonical/1 and write_term/2
without the option write `'$VAR'(1)` as it is, as swipl's do.

CHARACTER ESCAPES, a fifth bit of the writer's mode word (16), carried down
with quoted, ignore_ops and numbervars (`mode & 27`, where it was 11) and
read where an atom is written (`mode & 17`): a quote inside an atom is
`\'`, and 7, 8, 11 and 12 are `\a` `\b` `\v` `\f` in an atom and a string,
13 `\r` in a string as an atom always had it (`coco_escape_letter`). SET BY
THE WRITES A PROGRAM ASKS FOR, through `coco_write_mode`: writeq/1 and `~q`
25, print/1 and `~p` 25, write_canonical/1 17, write_term/2's
`quoted(true)` 17. NOT by the engine's own: the store's text, a channel's,
the journal's, a message, the REPL's answer and term_to_atom/2 keep the
doubled quote -- swipl's term_to_atom/2 doubles it too (and writes a newline
as it is, where this writes `\n`), and the store reads back unchanged, a
store written by 2.2.4 and one by 2.2.5 holding the same text. The other
control characters, which swipl writes `\x1\` (and print/1 `\u0001`), stay
as they are: this reader has no `\x..\` escape to read one back (cocolint
E1).

cocolint's X3 matched the text `numbervars(` anywhere, so write_term/2's
option -- now one -- was a HARD finding: X3 takes numbervars before any
argument but `true` or `false` (`notword/1`), and still finds numbervars/3.

## A call sees the clauses that stood when it began (2.3.0)

An outside review (2026-10-17) found README.md claiming what the engine did
not do, and 0614894 made the claims true of 2.2.5: a retry read the live
clause list. The owner chose to fix the engine. Through 2.2.5 a retract or an
assert while a call on its predicate was open moved the clauses that call had
still to try: `( q(X), write(X), nl, retract(q(1)), fail ; true )` over
`q(1). q(2). q(3).` printed 1 and 3, `forall(q(X), retract(q(X)))` over five
clauses left two, and `forall(seen(_), assertz(seen(copied)))` never ended,
the open call meeting every clause it asserted. ISO's logical update view,
which swipl keeps, gives a call the clauses that stood when it began, whatever
is asserted or retracted while it is open, and a NEW call the clauses as they
are. It is this engine's now.

THE END OF WHAT A CALL MAY TRY. A clause frame keeps `cend`, its predicate's
clause count when the call began, in four bytes the alignment had left free
(the frame is no bigger), set at both pushes (`coco_regs_choice`, and the
step's own in `coco_engine_run`). A selection takes no candidate at or past
it -- one compare, where the old one asked for `coco_no_clause` -- so an
assertz lies past every open call's end. An asserta moves every open frame on
by a clause, its next clause and its end (`coco_frames_on`, act 2), as it
moves the clauses.

A CLAUSE RETRACTED UNDER AN OPEN CALL DIES IN PLACE. With a frame open on its
predicate a retract takes nothing out: the clause keeps its position, marked
with the number of its death (`tomb[i]`, one past the last, `tera`), and each
open frame that has lived through no death is given that number as its first
(`fera`, stamped at the death by `coco_tomb_open`; not at the push, which every
call that leaves a choice makes, where a death under an open call is rare). A
frame tries a dead clause that died at or after its first, and a new call
tries none. The index keeps the position, as it keeps every other; the
database loses the clause at once (the backend's sync skips the dead,
`coco_zg_sync_pred`). The dead are swept out -- the positions closed up, the
index dropped (`coco_pred_sweep`) -- once no frame is open on the predicate:
at its next retract, assert or reconsult, at every 256th call that meets them,
in `'$pred_count'`, and at the start of each query a host starts with nothing
running and the collector on (`coco_tomb_sweep_all`, over the store's list of
the predicates that have dead, `tpreds`), the collector's own vouch that
nothing else on the machine is waiting to go on. Which frames are open is a
walk of the engines on the machine's chain over the same store, `m->eng` and
each `outer` -- every engine a program can still fail back into, as no
builtin leaves a choice point behind -- and a predicate no frame was pushed
on since a walk found none walks nothing (`framed`). A reconsult would do the
same with a file's clauses, the new ones after the dead, but none runs under
an open call: a reconsult is a command.

THE PROBE STILL TESTS ITS COUNT ONCE. Every call that may be deterministic
asks the probe for its first candidate and whether there is a second, and a
predicate with dead clauses must answer from the live ones. A test of
`ntomb` beside the probe's test of its count was a load and a branch a call,
nrev +0.64 % of 2.2.5's instructions. The probe reads `nprobe` instead, a
copy of the count in the four bytes after `arity` while no clause is dead and
0 while one is (`coco_pred_nprobe`, after every write of either count), so its
one test of its count sends an empty predicate and one with dead clauses
alike out of line (`coco_pred_probe_cold`, weak). The selection asks `ntomb`
once a retry and takes a predicate with dead clauses out of line too
(`coco_select_dead`, weak: inlined, it cost every retry its registers, queens
+1.3 %).

THE READERS of the clause list as the predicate's clauses skip the dead:
listing/1, clause/2 (by live ordinal, `coco_pred_live_at`, which keeps where
its last answer was, so an enumeration among dead clauses takes a step a
clause and not a walk), predicate_property/2's counts, the recorder's tried
heads, the backtrace's search for a clause by its code, and the store's sync.

THE FREEZE keeps the owner's design (2026-10-17): a frozen machine records no
revision of the knowledge base, which other machines may use and change while
it is frozen. A frame's next clause and its end are written as counts of LIVE
clauses -- the next clause in section `C` as before, the end in a new section
`L`, after `N` -- because the base a thaw reloads holds no dead
(`coco_pred_live_before`). A blob without `L`, 2.2.5's, leaves each end at
4294967295 until the resumed run has loaded the modules' own clauses back, and
the run then binds it to the clauses there are (`coco_frames_bound`): bound at
the restore, member/2's frames met an empty predicate. An embedded store that
no other machine uses resumes where it stopped but for one thing: a clause
retracted AHEAD of an open call is gone from the store, so the thawed call
does not meet it where a run never frozen would.

`test/files/update_view.pl` holds 34 cases to swipl 9.0.4, 55 lines byte for
byte -- a retract ahead of an open call and behind it, an assertz and an
asserta under one, a new call, the same clause retracted twice, a cut and a
throw through an open call, a retracted rule that still runs for the call
that saw it, a worklist read by a loop and by a recursion, a counter beside an
open call, a table indexed on its first argument and on its second, 300
deaths with sweeps between them and the predicate filled again, an outer
search open while an inner one changes the predicate, a call's own clause
retracted from its body, a new call whose key leaves one candidate and that
one dead, and the last clause retracted and then asked for by its key. Run
one at a time, 2.2.5 writes another text for 24 of them and runs one for ever
(u07, an asserta under an open call, which met its own clause again at every
retry). `test/engine.pl`'s new section runs three programs whole and thawed
at every 50 inferences, each turn a process (a clause retracted behind the
call, one ahead of it, the clauses the call asserts itself), and a clause
retracted under a call the run then cuts away read by a second process. Lesson
basics/07 says it and checks it, and through 2.2.5 its new section ran for
ever.

An arm takes one rule out each, and each goes red:

| arm | red |
|---|---|
| no end at the push (`cend`) | files, engine, lesson 07 (runs for ever) |
| no first death a frame lived through (`fera`) | files, engine, lesson 07 |
| an asserta that moves no open frame | files |
| an asserta that moves the next clause and not the end | files |
| a sync that writes the dead | engine (stepped, and the cut read by a second process) |
| a freeze that writes the next clause as a position | engine (stepped) |
| clause/2 by position, not by live ordinal | files |
| a probe that takes a dead candidate | files (u32, u33) |
| a selection that takes the dead | files, engine, lesson 07 |
| a push that leaves `framed` clear | files, engine, lesson 07 |
| a restore that leaves `framed` clear | engine (stepped) |
| no `L` section | engine (stepped) |
| a retract that takes a clause out and leaves `nprobe` | files (u34) |

and two more, read by hand from machines 2.2.5 froze part way through and
this binary thawed and stepped to the end: an end bound at the restore, before
the run has loaded the modules' own clauses back, leaves a member/2 open over
a list nothing more to try (the fixture prints `a` where its run prints
`g(3)`), and an end never bound lets a call meet the clauses it asserted under
itself (`1 2 3 4 6 7 8 9`, where the bound end stops at the `6` that 2.2.5's
turns had asserted before the freeze). Three are costs, and measured: `nprobe`
not kept by an assert sends every call's probe out of line (zero.sh, work less
padding: nrev +13.7 %, queens +6.7 %, lookup +5.9 %); no sweep at every 256th
call that meets the dead leaves a predicate read after one death paying for it
at every call (`k(1)` called 200 000 times after `k(2)` died under a call then
cut away: 312 136 538 instructions to 333 360 235); and no sweep at a query's
start leaves the dead to the next query's calls (the REPL, the same death and
200 calls in the next query: 20 612 429 to 20 654 836). No arm:
`'$pred_count'`'s sweep (no answer depends on it), the reconsult's dead in
place (no program can reach it: a reconsult is a command, and `use_module/1`
and `ensure_loaded/1` load a file once), and the dead skipped by listing/1,
the recorder, the backtrace and predicate_property/2, each read by hand.

THE COST. `tools/flow/zero.sh` against 2.2.5, work less padding: nrev
66 480 221 to 66 694 337 instructions (+0.32 %; by callgrind's counts per
function the step loop +111 206 and the probe +105 061, about one
instruction each a call, the probe being handed the machine), queens
41 777 200 to 42 211 708 (+1.04 %: the selection +101 285, `ntomb` read at
every retry, and the step loop +164 146, the end and `framed` stored at every
push), lookup 47 590 133 to 47 682 815 (+0.19 %). The clock, eleven alternating
rounds of user time, medians: as built, nrev +10.3 %, queens +0.1 %, lookup
+3.3 %; built with every function on a 64-byte line (`-falign-functions=64`,
2.2.5 and this alike, scratch builds), nrev +1.9 %, queens +5.3 %, lookup
+1.8 %. So nrev's 10 % is placement, as 1.9.5's and 1.13.0's were, and the
alignment, which moves queens as much the other way, is not proposed. Two
diagnostic builds of the first cut, which tested `ntomb` in the probe, say the
same: with the test taken out (wrong, and timed only) nrev ran at 2.2.5's
time, and with the probe's new argument taken out instead and the test left
in, 8 % slower.

A PREDICATE CHANGED OVER AND OVER UNDER ONE CALL OPEN ON IT keeps its dead
until that call ends, and every retract or new call of it walks them: `w(X)`
left open over two clauses while `retract(w(_)), assertz(w(N))` runs 40 000
times takes 0.643 s, where 2.2.5 took 0.015 s (handing the open call the wrong
clauses) and swipl 9.0.4 takes 6.646 s, walking its erased clauses the same
way -- and with no call open as well, where it takes 6.127 s, this binary
0.016 s and 2.2.5 0.025 s. 10 000 and 20 000 rounds take 0.037 s and 0.226 s
here (one run each, the process's CPU time).

NOT SWI's: clause/2 holds no call open on the predicate it reads -- it is
`'$pred_count'/3`, between/3 and `'$clause'/3`, the count taken once and each
clause read by its live ordinal -- so a change it makes to the predicate
during its own enumeration moves what it reads next: a retract of the first
clause as it is read gives `[1,3]` over `q(1). q(2). q(3).` and an asserta
`[1,1,1]`, swipl's `[1,2,3]` both (COMPAT.md). A clause/2 that only reads, or
reads a predicate another call changes, is right.

## A Unix domain socket is an address (2.4.0)

Asked by the owner (2026-10-18): the HTTP libraries over a Unix domain socket.
None of them held a socket of its own -- library(http) is a grammar over bytes,
library(httpd) five transport predicates over library(tcp) or library(tls),
library(websocket) clauses over the same two, library(curl) libcurl's -- so the
work is the socket seam's, and two client options.

THE ADDRESS. `unix(Path)` stands where a port stands: `tcp_listen(unix(Path), S)`,
and a new `tcp_connect(+Address, -Conn)` takes `unix(Path)` or `Host:Port` (which
is `tcp_connect/3` spelt as one term). Everything after is the same slot, the
same reads and writes, the same close, so `httpd_serve(unix(Path), Options)`
serves -- pages, keep-alive, the pool, websocket pages -- with no change to
library(httpd) but a refusal of `tls(...)` there, by name (a socket file's
permissions are its access control, and library(tls) dials TCP). The clients go
as `curl --unix-socket` does, the URL naming the Host header and the path:
library(curl)'s `unix_socket(Path)` (CURLOPT_UNIX_SOCKET_PATH, libcurl 7.40) and
`ws_open/3`'s, ws:// only (with wss:// a domain error). A peer accepted on one is
the atom `'unix:'` -- nginx's `$remote_addr` for it -- and the path the client
bound after the colon, which a client seldom does.

THE FILE, three decisions. A bind that meets the name (EADDRINUSE) asks whether
anybody listens: only if the name is a SOCKET (lstat, never followed) and a
non-blocking connect to it is refused is the file a leftover, unlinked and bound
again; a live server's file is refused and left alone (its server sees the
question as a connection that closes at once), and so is a regular file, a
directory or a link of that name. Python's asyncio unlinks any socket it finds,
a live server's too, and Go unlinks nothing and fails. On Linux a listener whose
backlog is full answers the non-blocking connect EAGAIN, and is alive; BSD and
macOS answer it ECONNREFUSED, as they answer a dead one (`sonewconn` failing in
`unp_connect`), so there a listener that busy at that moment can lose its file
to a second listen. Not tested here: this box is Linux. The listener's close
removes its file first, as Go's does, then closes -- and only while the name is
still the socket it bound, by device and inode (`coco_t_dev`, `coco_t_ino`), so a
server that has taken the path since keeps its own. Who may connect is the
file's business: the umask the process has when it listens, and the
directory's permissions. Not here, and said in the module's header: Linux's
abstract names (`@name`), descriptors passed over a socket (SCM_RIGHTS) and the
peer's credentials (SO_PEERCRED).

THE BINDINGS, both a line, neither pasted C. Cicili's std declares AF_UNIX beside
AF_INET but has no `<sys/un.h>`, so `modules/tcp/binding.cicili` declares `struct
sockaddr_un` in an init-macro that emits nothing, as `modules/clay/binding.cicili`
does Clay's; the struct is the header's, and the module asks `sizeof` of its
`sun_path` (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS: a path of one to 107 or 103, longer
a domain error, never cut short). `lib/net/curl.cicili` names no unix-socket
option word and declares `curl_easy_setopt` for exactly such an option, so
`modules/curl/binding.cicili` names the constant and `cl_p_do` sets it through
that call. Both are written as the files Cicili's tree would hold, and kept here
because that tree is frozen from this side.

TWO SMALL THINGS IN THE SAME FILE, found on the way. tcp_why/1 answers why a
connect or a listen failed as well as a read (the errno text, or getaddrinfo's
for a name it could not find): ws_open/3 builds its reason from it, and through
2.3.0 said `cannot connect to 127.0.0.1:18799 ()`, the reason being the last
read's, here none; now `(Connection refused)`. And a connect, an accept or a
listen whose variable will not take the slot gives it back: through 2.3.0 the
socket stayed open in a slot nobody held (`tcp_connect(H, P, 99)` that failed,
one more slot gone a call). Lesson 20 named an option `insecure(true)` that
library(curl) has not got; it is `verify_peer(false)`.

PROVED: test/tcp.pl's three new sections, 16 checks -- a round trip over a socket
file with a NUL and 0xFF both ways, the file made by the listen and kept by a
connection's close and removed by the listener's, the errors by name, a live
server refused and still serving, a regular file refused and unchanged, a name
taken over left to its new server, and a second cocolog killed (9) while it
listened, whose file this process then replaces -- with thirteen arms, one rule
out each, all red at their check: no leftover replaced, any file taken for a
leftover, any socket taken for one, no unlink at the close, no inode check, the
take's and the accept's slot kept, the length check out (the struct overflowed),
the peer's `unix:`, the unix connect's reason, the TCP connect's reason, the
`Host:Port` form. test/httpd.pl: httpd on a socket file reached by raw bytes,
two requests down one connection, and the system's `curl --unix-socket`, the
file gone with the server, and `tls(...)` refused; test/curl.pl: library(curl)'s
`unix_socket(Path)` to a server on a socket file; test/websocket.pl: a session
over one, the reason naming the file, wss:// refused -- five arms more, each
red: httpd's refusal out, ws_open's option, its wss:// refusal, its reason's
`unix:`, curl's option. NOT ARMED: the probe's O_NONBLOCK (only a listener whose
backlog is full shows it; blocking, the second listen would wait for the first
to accept) and TCP_NODELAY left off a unix socket (the setsockopt fails, and
nothing reads its answer). Lessons 16, 17, 20 and 49 say it and check it.

THE COST is the module's, none the engine's (lib/ is untouched): an address
shape asked at each listen and connect/2, a flag read at each accept, nothing at
a read or a write; and tcp.so's static table, four rows more a slot and the
peer's row 128 bytes wide, 17 432 bytes of bss to 40 984.

Green on 2.4.0's modules, with the server up: tcp, http, httpd, httpd-tls, curl,
websocket, tunnel, units, zigurat-tls, flowchart (its tables rebuilt) and lint;
lessons 16, 17, 20 and 49. The suite on 2.4.0, the server up: 70 lines, red 0,
5 SKIP (tensors, torch-graph, torch-grad, torch-replay, tensorflow: no CUDA on
this box).

## A read that failed raises, A* reopens, and two quieter faults (2.11.1)

An outside review of 885f9b7 (2.11.0) made four findings, and each held when it
was checked against the code and reproduced where it could be. The owner's
word: fix them all, and raise `resource_error` for the failed read.

THE READ. A predicate's clauses come from the backend the first time
something asks for them (`coco_pred_ensure`). Through 2.11.0 the store marked
the predicate read BEFORE it asked, kept whatever the fetch had put in when it
stopped, and no caller looked at the answer. The Zigurat fetch passed over a
row it could not read, so the predicate answered from the rest in silence, and
the next write -- the backend writes a predicate back whole
(`coco_zg_sync_pred`) -- rewrote it from that copy. The database lost the row.
Reproduced on the server with two clauses and a row beside them that reads as
no clause: one `assertz`, and the row was gone. A read is now all of a
predicate or none:

- **Nothing of a failed read is kept.** The clauses the fetch added are cut
  back (`coco_pred_cut_back`: their programs, the count, the index), their
  cells counted dead, `loaded` set back so the next call asks again, and
  `empty_fetch` left alone, so the pre-warm never takes a failure for an
  absence.
- **The reason travels on the store** (`fetch_err`, `fetch_pi`, `fetch_oom`),
  and `coco_fetch_error` raises `error(resource_error(knowledge_base),
  context(Name/Arity, Why))` from it, or `error(resource_error(memory), _)`
  when memory is what ran out.
- **Every reader raises it**: a call, from either of the step's paths;
  `clause/2`, `predicate_property/2`, `listing/0,1`, `abolish/1`, `retract/1`
  and the clause count.
- **Every writer refuses before it touches the predicate**: `assertz/1` and
  `asserta/1` raise it, and a consult reports it as it reports a clause too
  long for a row and goes on.
- **A thaw refuses, saying why.**
- **The text is SWI's shape for a resource error with a context**:
  `p/1: Not enough resources: knowledge_base (the row at ordinal 1000 does not
  read as a clause)`.

Both backends say which row. The Zigurat fetch reads the whole answer before
it puts a clause in, and names what failed: the call, the answer, a row's
ordinal or its clause, memory for the rows, a row that does not read, a row
the store would not take. Zeytun's requires its `END` line and stops at the
first row it cannot read. And the embedded store, which wrote through a null
pointer when an allocation was refused inside a procedure, throws
`std::bad_alloc` there and rolls back in `ce_exec`, as it does for any refusal.

THE STEP, AND WHAT A BRANCH IN IT COST. The first cut tested
`coco_pred_ensure`'s answer in the step loop. Clang's estimate gave the
failure 3/8 of every call's path (the zero heuristic). That put the loop's
calls of `coco_push_choice` and `coco_arg_key` under its threshold for a cold
call site, 45 against the 225 a hot one gets (`-Rpass-missed=inline` on the
emitted `cocolog.c` names it), and left both out of line. In work less
padding (`tools/flow/zero.sh`) that was queens +3.1 %, nrev +0.8 % and lookup
+0.7 % against 2.11.0. Two attempts changed nothing:

- Moving the raise out of line (`coco_fetch_error_regs` and `_goal`, weak):
  the counts were identical to the instruction.
- `__builtin_expect` in an inline helper: it is lowered before inlining, so
  there was no branch left to carry it.

What paid is `coco_pred_ready` (weak). It answers the clause count, or 0 after
a failed read, and the step tests it where it always tested the count, so the
path for a predicate with clauses has no branch it did not have. The failure
is caught on the path for a predicate with no clauses, ahead of the dynamic
arm, by `loaded` being 0. Its first build called `coco_pred_ensure` from
inside, two calls a call: nrev +2.6 %. Answering a predicate read already
itself, against 2.11.0 the work less padding is lower on all three:

| program | 2.11.0 | 2.11.1 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| nrev | 68 667 404 | 67 832 595 | −1.22 % |
| queens | 43 004 563 | 42 908 436 | −0.22 % |
| lookup | 48 879 636 | 48 579 793 | −0.61 % |

The step compares the count the call returned instead of loading it, and the
fast path has no bound test.

THE GROWTHS. Fifteen places in the source set a pointer straight from
`realloc` (`x = realloc(x, n)`). A refused growth then lost the block and the
code went on through null. The Zigurat fetch crashed so, which is the
review's case. The others were:

- Zeytun's fetch;
- the reader's list and argument buffers, four sites each emitted twice, which
  now fail the read with `out of memory reading a list` or `... an argument
  list`;
- library(text)'s output buffer, five sites that are one grow function now;
- torch's CSV reader;
- library(process)'s output buffer;
- the embedded store's token and id arrays.

Each grows through a second pointer and raises memory. NOT TESTED by a check:
one site's growth cannot be refused from Prolog without the engine's own
growths being refused first (the `ulimit -v` cases of test/errors.pl reach
those).

THE RUNNER. Through 2.11.0, test/run.pl gave a test binary its verdict from
the last line it printed, so a binary that printed GREEN and then crashed on
its way out was green. Now GREEN or SKIP counts only with exit status 0
(`binary_verdict/3` in the prelude), and a red line names the status.

A*. `astar/6` and `astar/7` closed an expanded node for good, which is right
only for a CONSISTENT heuristic. An admissible one that was not consistent got
a dearer path than `shortest_path/5` gives: the review's graph answered s-a-g
at 5, where s-b-a-g costs 4. The search now reopens: it keeps the cheapest
cost found for each node (`Best`) and the cost each was expanded at (`Done`).
A node popped at a cost below the one it was expanded at is expanded again,
and a child no cheaper than the best known is not put on the open list.
`astar/7` marks each node once, however many times it is expanded, and a node
the caller marked before the search is never searched. Measured over 1444
pairs on a costed hex disk of radius 5 with five walls:

- **A consistent heuristic (`hex_distance`) gives exactly 2.11.0's answers.**
  Four searches a pair (costed, unit, `astar/7` with the caller's set, and
  `shortest_path/5`) give the same paths and costs byte for byte, in fewer
  inferences: 22 195 537 against 29 484 760 for the costed search over all
  pairs. 2.11.0 pushed entries a cheaper one had already beaten and threw
  them away at the pop; without the pruning, the new search takes 33 590 471.
- **An admissible heuristic that is not consistent** (the distance halved on
  odd columns): 2.11.0 answered a dearer cost than `shortest_path/5` for 2 of
  the 1444 pairs, and 2.11.1 for none, in 62 147 750 inferences against
  86 775 417 (each search and its oracle).

## A growth is cold, and the clause runner is faster for it (2.11.2)

The owner's word: add `(cold)` to Cicili and fix the slowdown. The slowdown
is one 1.10.28 recorded and 2.11.1 met again. A rare path's call in a hot
function weighs, in clang's eyes, what its guess gives the test in front of
it. 1.10.28 put the growth fallback out of line and weak, so that a push
would not inline a refused doubling's second try. The block that calls it
was still weighed as clang guesses a comparison, and naive reverse paid
+0.63 %, all of it in `coco_clause_run_r`, whose heap tests now carried a
call. 2.11.1's first cut of the failed read cost queens +3.1 % the same
way. The C has an answer, the attribute on the callee, and Cicili had no
word for it.

CICILI 3.1.0 (`cc24ae0`, let in by name) writes `__attribute__((cold))` for
`(cold)`, before a definition and before a `(decl)` prototype.

- Clang takes a block that calls a cold function as unlikely. It lays the
  caller's hot path out without it, and weighs the caller's other calls for
  inlining without its weight.
- The function itself is optimised for size, inlined only if it is tiny, and
  put in `.text.unlikely`.
- `(weak) (cold)` is allowed; `(inline) (cold)` is refused.
- cocolog 2.11.1, which writes no `(cold)`, transpiles byte for byte as it
  did under 3.0.0. 2.11.2 needs 3.1.0: an older Cicili stops at `unknown
  symbol: cold`.

THE ARMS. Each arm is 2.11.1's emitted `cocolog.c` with
`__attribute__((cold))` put before the named functions' definitions and
prototypes -- what 3.1.0 writes for `(cold)` -- compiled and linked as the
Makefile does, 12 s an arm. Each is measured against the same C unmarked,
in work less padding (`tools/flow/zero.sh`):

| arm | marked cold | nrev | queens | lookup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G | the growths: `coco_grow_slow`, `coco_eng_grow_slow`, `coco_grow_short` | −1.22 % | −0.30 % | −0.58 % |
| G2 | G without `coco_grow_short` | −1.20 % | −0.30 % | −0.58 % |
| E | the raisers: `coco_raise`, `coco_throw`, `coco_fail_err`, `coco_mem_error`, `coco_bt_capture`, the six `coco_*_error`s, the three integer errors, the failed read's three, `coco_halted_step` (18) | −0.00 % | −0.05 % | +0.82 % |
| F | the failed read's three raisers and `coco_halted_step` | −0.16 % | −0.25 % | +0.17 % |
| T | the tracer and the recorder (16) | −0.17 % | −0.50 % | +0.17 % |
| L | `coco_limit_go` | −0.16 % | −0.32 % | +0.17 % |
| GT | G and T | −1.37 % | −0.93 % | −0.41 % |
| GL | G and L | −1.37 % | −0.97 % | −0.41 % |
| GF | G and F | −1.19 % | −0.21 % | −0.58 % |
| GE | G and E | −1.20 % | −0.43 % | +0.21 % |
| GTLF | G, T, L and F | −1.22 % | −0.29 % | −0.58 % |
| GD | G and the dead-clause paths (`coco_pred_probe_cold`, `coco_pred_probe_dead`, `coco_select_dead`) | −1.20 % | −0.30 % | −0.58 % |

G is shipped, and nothing else:

- **G moves all three programs the same way, and it is the slowdown asked
  about.** The per-function count says where: `coco_clause_run_r` ran 2.0 %
  fewer instructions on naive reverse (45 298 362 to 44 381 102), and the
  step loop the same to 71 instructions. 1.10.28's +0.63 % is taken back and
  more.
- **E made lookup dearer**, all of it in the step loop: `coco_engine_run` ran
  3.3 % more instructions (16 392 247 to 16 928 080).
- **T, L and F alone each moved nrev about −0.17 % and lookup +0.17 % alike.**
  Three unrelated sets of functions giving the same numbers is the step
  loop's registers and layout moving, not anything the markings say.
- **GT and GL are a trade that does not survive the next edit.** Each beat G
  on nrev and on queens (queens's step loop ran 6 333 064 instructions to
  6 023 041 under GL, −4.9 %) and lost to it on lookup. With F beside them
  (GTLF) the gain was gone: G's numbers to within 0.02 %.
- **D moved nothing.** The dead-clause paths were already out of line and
  weak.

THE FIRST CUT AGAIN. 2.11.1's first cut tested `coco_pred_ensure`'s answer in
the step loop, and clang left `coco_push_choice` and `coco_arg_key` out of
line. Rebuilt from its saved C and measured against 2.11.1, in work less
padding:

| | nrev | queens | lookup |
|---|---|---|---|
| the first cut | +2.02 % | +3.30 % | +1.28 % |
| its raise cold (F) | +2.01 % | +0.70 % | +1.36 % |
| its raise and the growths cold | +0.79 % | +0.38 % | +0.78 % |

- With its raise cold, both helpers are inline again: `objdump` finds no
  call of either in `coco_engine_run`, where the first cut has one of each.
- Queens's cost is then down to 0.70 %, but nrev and lookup keep theirs.
  Against G alone the first cut still costs +2.0 %, +0.7 % and +1.4 %.
- 2.11.1's fold stays. A test folded into one the loop already makes costs
  nothing; `(cold)` is for the call that cannot be folded.

THE CLOCK says nothing either way. The same binary against itself, in seven
alternating pairs of user time, read 0.959, 0.954 and 1.085 (nrev, queens,
lookup). G against the unmarked C read 0.936, 0.938 and 0.970 one way round,
and 1.005, 0.986 and 1.013 the other. The counts are the record.
