## The green world's cost was one call, and the step answers it inline (2.11.3)

The owner's word: find the slowness root. Run W (bench/README.md) counted
2.2.5 to 2.11.2 and found that the green world, 2.6.0 to 2.10.1, had cost
the single-threaded engine 1.1-2.3 % of its instructions, which no release
had counted as it landed.

THE BISECTION. All twelve releases from 2.5.1 to 2.10.1 were built from
their release commits, each in a worktree of its own, by this box's clang
and Cicili 3.1.0. They were counted in one invocation of
`tools/flow/zero.sh`, with 2.2.5, 2.11.1, 2.11.2 and this release beside
them. Work less padding:

| step | nrev | queens | lookup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.5.1 to 2.6.0, and 2.6.0 to 2.7.0 | −0.00 % | +0.00 % | +0.00 % |
| 2.7.0 to 2.8.0 | −0.34 % | +0.00 % | +0.01 % |
| 2.8.0 to 2.8.1 | +0.00 % | +0.00 % | +0.03 % |
| **2.8.1 to 2.9.0** | **+2.53 %** | **+1.39 %** | **+1.13 %** |
| 2.9.0 to 2.10.1, six releases | −0.00 % | −0.00 % | −0.03 % |
| 2.10.1 to 2.11.1 | −1.21 % | −0.22 % | −0.60 % |
| 2.11.1 to 2.11.2 | −1.22 % | −0.30 % | −0.60 % |
| **2.11.2 to 2.11.3** | **−1.87 %** | **−0.73 %** | **−0.98 %** |

The cost is one release. 2.8.0's −0.34 % on nrev is `memcpy` alone, two
calls fewer in the reps (−229 408), not the step loop.

THE ROOT, read per function: callgrind's self instructions and the calls
into each function, the reps less none, as zero.sh counts the whole.

- **Through 2.8.1, `coco_pred_ensure` costs nothing of its own and is never
  called.** Clang inlined it into `coco_engine_run`, so a call of a plain
  predicate paid only its first two tests: out of range, and loaded.
- **2.9.0 put the write barrier into it**, `coco_g_write_begin` bound with a
  `defer` of `coco_g_write_end_cleanup` after those two tests. The bigger
  body was no longer inlined. It is called once for every call of a plain
  predicate, at 19 instructions:
  - nrev: 105 060 calls, 1 996 140 instructions;
  - queens: 28 885 calls;
  - lookup: 40 040 calls;
  - the counting loop: 400 008 calls, 7 600 152 instructions.

  The step loop itself ran a few fewer instructions with the body gone
  (nrev −96 972).
- **Nothing else of 2.9.0 counts.** The barrier on findall's puts
  (`coco_store_put`: 92 a search of queens, 37 instructions each) and on a
  clause's first compile (1 003 in lookup) cost thousands of instructions,
  not millions.
- **2.11.1 made the step's call `coco_pred_ready` (weak)**, 12 instructions
  a call: its −1.21 %, −0.22 % and −0.60 % above. It was still a call for
  every call.

THE FIX. `coco_pred_count` (lib/kb.cicili) is `(static) (inline)`. A
predicate read already answers its clause count there, inline. One not read
yet -- its first call, or the next after a read that failed -- calls
`coco_pred_ready`, now `(weak) (cold)`. The step's two sites call
`coco_pred_count`, and what each answers is what `coco_pred_ready` answered.
Against 2.11.2, per function:

- `coco_pred_ready`'s whole cost goes. On nrev it was 1 260 720
  instructions; on queens 346 630 become 34, the two calls of a first read.
- `coco_engine_run` runs a few instructions FEWER: nrev −2 044, lookup
  −40 043, queens's nested engine −55 783, the loop 0.
- Nothing new is called out of line. `coco_push_choice` and `coco_arg_key`,
  the two 2.11.1 saw pushed out, stay inline.

The counting loop, `main(100000,4)` less `main(100000,0)` with its padding,
falls from 78 740 972 instructions a rep on 2.11.2 to 77 540 938 (−1.52 %).
2.8.1 ran 77 940 935.

WHERE IT STANDS:

- Against 2.8.1, the last release before the barrier: nrev −1.83 %, queens
  +0.12 %, lookup −1.07 %, the loop −0.51 %.
- Against Run U's 2.2.5: nrev −1.10 %, queens +1.64 %, lookup +0.48 %, the
  loop −0.24 %. What is left above 2.2.5 is 2.3.0's update view and 2.5.0's
  rational tag (2.2.5 to 2.5.1: +1.09 %, +1.52 %, +1.53 %), each counted
  when it landed.

THE CLOCK says nothing either way. Ten alternating pairs of user time,
2.11.3 against 2.11.2 at the bench's reps, read 0.951 (nrev), 0.990
(queens), 1.042 (the loop), 0.956 (lookup) and 1.060 (sortnums). The counts
are the record.

THE LESSON. A barrier, a lock or a `defer` added to a function the step loop
calls can take that function out of line. The cost then lands in every call,
while the function's own code reads as unchanged. 2.9.0 proved its barrier
with cases, a concurrency stress and the full suite, and counted no zero.sh.
CLAUDE.md now says to count it.

PROVED:

## A file's time to the nanosecond (2.12.2)

cicilang's feedback, item 1 of three: `time_file/2` answered whole seconds,
`st_mtime` cast to a float. Two writes inside one second had the same time,
and a tool asking which of two files is newer (a build's "is the output
stale") got "neither". swipl 9.0.4 answers `tv_sec + tv_nsec / 1e9` of
`st_mtim` (`LastModifiedFile` in its `pl-files.c`), and so does this now.

Darwin's `struct stat` names the field `st_mtimespec` and has no `st_mtim`
(xnu's `bsd/sys/stat.h`), and `st_mtim` is the one member swipl's configure
looks for (`HAVE_STRUCT_STAT_ST_MTIM`). So swipl on a Mac answers whole
seconds and cocolog the nanoseconds: a difference by choice, the reason the
feedback gave holding there as well.

The fields are Cicili 3.3.0's (49d0f12, pushed with the owner's leave):
`stat_t` declares `st_atim`, `st_mtim`, `st_ctim` and Darwin's three
`st_*timespec`. A declaration emits nothing, and a target picks its spelling
under `@ifdef __APPLE__`. cocolog needs it from here on: 3.2.0 stops at
`unknown member: st_mtim of type: stat_t`. On 3.3.0, 2.12.1's source emitted
the same C as on 3.2.0, all 23 files byte for byte, and coco's 10 too.

PROVED:

- Five files, swipl 9.0.4 and cocolog to the last digit:
  - a file touched at `2026-10-28T12:00:00.75Z` is `1793188800.75` in both;
  - four real files carry their nine or ten digits of fraction.
- `test/files/stat.pl` prints that fixture's time, which the harness stamps
  for both runs (a whole second on Darwin, where swipl reads none). Result:
  agrees with SWI, 16 lines. 2.12.1 answered `1793188800.0` there.
- The rest:
  - `test/files.pl` is green over all its cases;
  - lesson 03 ends `done`;
  - the two changed files lint clean;
  - the card's cites are all anchored.

## consult/1, load_files/2 and `[File]` as goals (2.13.0)

cicilang's feedback, item 3: a program that loaded a file at run time
stopped at `existence_error(procedure, consult/1)`. None of SWI's three
loading goals existed. cicilang loads with ensure_loaded/1, so for it this
is compatibility only.

WHAT THEY DO:

- **They consult.** The file goes into the knowledge base, written through
  as `cocolog run` writes it, and its clauses from the last time are
  replaced (SWI's reconsult). Its directives run each time it is read.
- **`library(Name)`** is the library loader's, whatever the call.
- **`load_files/2`'s options:**
  - `if(true)` is the default.
  - `if(changed)` compares the file's `time_file/2` with the one the store
    read it at.
  - `if(exists)` loads nothing for a file that is not there.
  - `if(not_loaded)` and `must_be_module(true)` go through the module
    loader, as ensure_loaded/1 and use_module/1 do; SWI says they are those.
  - Any other option is ignored, as SWI ignores one it does not know.
- **SWI's shapes, read off swipl 9.0.4:**
  - An unbound file and a partial option list are instantiation errors.
  - An option list that is no list is a type error naming its tail.
  - A missing file is `existence_error(source_sink, F)`, and a directory
    `existence_error(file, F)`.
  - A single file's error is raised. In a list, each file's error is
    printed and the next file loads. A ball that is no `error/2`, and a
    signal (cocolog delivers one as `error(signal(Name, Num), _)`), are
    thrown on, so a Ctrl-C stops a list of loads.
- **The shape.** A Coco half in `lib/library.cicili` walks the list and
  reads the options over one C row, `'$lf_file'/2`. The files still to load
  ride on the engine's continuation, which a collection in one file's
  directives moves, rather than in a C frame's cells.

NO FILE IS LOADED TWICE BY TWO ROADS, a fault older than this release:

- `run F` and then ensure_loaded/1 of F read F twice, into the store and
  as a module.
- So did use_module/1 under two spellings of one path.
- Every clause then answered twice.

The fix:

- The store keeps the files read into it (`loads`: the real path and
  `time_file/2`). Every consult a host makes notes its file before the
  read: `run`, the `consult` command, the toplevel, the goals.
- The module loader answers a file the store holds, or one a module was
  read from under another spelling, as loaded.
- consult/1 of a file loaded as a module is that load. This includes a
  `-s` program consulting itself. (Through 2.13; since 2.14.0 it reads the
  file again as that module.)
- A consult that a module's own load runs is the program's. Inside a
  module's load (an `-s` file's initialization/1) the store is muted, and
  a muted read keeps no origins: the first build's second consult there
  appended, `[1,1]`. The goal now unmutes the store around its own read
  and puts it back after.

WHERE IT DIFFERS FROM swipl, by choice:

- A syntax error ends the consult (the one thing that does), so the
  clauses after it are not read; swipl reads on. Both report it and succeed.
- `must_be_module(true)` asks no module header. cocolog has none.
- A code list is one file's name, which is what `"file"` reads as under
  the `codes` default. swipl takes a list of codes as a list of files.
- A list inside the list is walked, so `consult(["a","b"])` loads two
  files under `codes`.
- A file loaded as a module is not read again by consult/1; swipl reloads
  it. Since 2.14.0 it is read again as that module (below).

NOT FIXED: ACROSS PROCESSES A FILE CAN STILL BE THERE TWICE, as it was
through 2.12. The table of loaded files is the process's, not the
database's.

- **The fault.** One process consults a file into a store (`run F`). A
  second process then loads F as a module: `-s F`, use_module/1 or
  ensure_loaded/1. The second process holds the store's rows beside the
  module's clauses, and every clause answers twice (`[1,2,1,2]`, probed on
  `--embed`).
- **Where 2.13.0 helps.** consult/1 in the second process replaces its
  own rows (`[1,2]`).
- **The first thought for a fix is wrong.** Hiding those rows when the
  predicate is fetched would lose them: the backend writes a predicate back
  whole, so the next write would delete the rows the read left out
  (2.11.1's partial read).
- **Where a fix must look.** It touches all three arrangements, and is a
  proposal for the owner.

PROVED:

- **`test/files/consult.pl`** agrees with swipl 9.0.4 over 38 lines: the
  reconsult, lists, `[F]`, a directive `:- [b].`, every option and error
  shape above, `if(not_loaded)`/`if(changed)`/ensure_loaded/1 after a
  consult, and directives and initialization/1 run again.
- **`test/reconsult.pl`'s four new sections:**
  - A goal-level consult writes through, and a second process that
    consulted nothing reads it (`--embed`).
  - One file by two roads is loaded once, five ways, and two consults
    inside a module's load leave one copy.
  - `if(changed)` reads a file again when only the fraction of its stamp
    moved (12:00:00.25 to .50), which 2.12.2's nanosecond time makes
    possible.
  - What will not load: raised alone, reported in a list in SWI's words,
    and a syntax error reported.
  - The case is green, with the wire half against the server.
- **An arm per duplicate rule, each red.** Each is a build with the rule
  taken out:
  - the store's record in the module loader: `run` and then
    ensure_loaded/1 answer `[1,2,1,2]`;
  - the module under another spelling: use_module/1 twice doubles;
  - the module check in `'$lf_file'`: the `-s` program consulting itself
    answers `[1,1]`;
  - the store unmuted around the goal's read: two consults in an `-s`
    file's initialization/1 answer `[1,1]`.
- **Lesson 00** says it and checks it, and ends `done`.
- **Narrow cases green:** flowchart (with `'$lf_file'/2` and `'$lf_say'/1`
  in `library/flow/modes.pl`), library, directives, files, repl, script,
  engine, errors.
- **The five test binaries that compile the store** (solve, module, state,
  shared, zigurat) are green.
- **Lint clean.** The card's eight moved cites are corrected, and all 42
  are anchored.
- **The suite on 2.13.0**, with a freshly restarted server up, and the
  lint case first (green, 2 minutes): 75 lines in 17 minutes.
  - Five SKIPs: tensors, torch-graph, torch-grad, torch-replay and
    tensorflow. This box has no libtorch and no TensorFlow.
  - One red, window's run-time check "findall/3's own over a hundred
    times member/2's". Probed 40 times alone, w_copy/1's copies cost
    findall/3 some 0.85 ms and member/2's three steps 1.4 to 2.4 us, a
    ratio of 361 to 798. One interruption of those steps fails it: a VM
    exit here is some 18 us.
  - The check now takes the best of five probes. A copy charged to

## A module's file, consulted, is read again as the module (2.14.0)

cicilang 0.223's report: a program ensure_loads a file, edits it, and calls
consult/1 to take the edit. 2.13.0 read nothing, because it took the consult
as the load already made. swipl 9.0.4 reloads the file: its new clauses
replace the old ones, and a predicate the new text no longer defines goes. So
does this now. Each rule below is swipl's `'$noload'` (its boot/init.pl) and
was probed against it.

WHAT IT DOES:

- **consult/1, `[File]` and load_files/2's `if(true)` read a module's file
  again, as that module.** The read is muted, as the module's load was. Its
  clauses stay this process's own and are never written through. The file's
  directives run again, and each clause is held once.
- **`if(changed)` and `if(exists)` read a file again only when it is NEWER
  than the text held.** This holds for a module's file and a consulted one
  alike. `if(not_loaded)`, ensure_loaded/1 and use_module/1 never read it
  again. Through 2.13, `if(changed)` read a file whose time was only OTHER,
  an older one too, and `if(exists)` read every file that was there.
- **A read of a file takes its clauses out of every predicate its new text
  no longer defines.** This applies to a consult and to a module alike.
  Calling such a predicate afterwards raises `existence_error`, as in swipl.
  A predicate the file declared dynamic keeps what the program asserted.
  Through 2.13 a reconsult replaced the clauses of the predicates the new
  text touched and left the rest.
- **`[File]` of one file is consult/1 of it** (swipl's
  `[X] :- !, consult(X).`), so a missing file raises. Through 2.13 it went
  through the list's walk, which reports a file's error and loads the next.
- **The toplevel's `[F].` and `consult(F).` are those goals.** Through 2.13
  the toplevel consulted the file itself, beside the module that held it,
  and each clause answered twice.

HOW:

- **A module's clauses are owned by its file** (`coco_consult_owner`). The
  registry keeps the file's real path, resolved once when the file is named
  (`coco_module_set_file`), and the time of the text it holds. Through 2.13 a
  module's clauses had no origin: no muted read kept one.
- **A forget takes only the clauses of the store's own mute**
  (`coco_pred_forget_from`). A muted re-read leaves alone a clause the same
  file wrote through, and a consult never touches a module's clauses.
- **A read notes the predicates it touched**, the set the reconsult already
  kept. At its end, every other predicate of the store that holds a clause
  of the file's origin, under the read's mute, loses those clauses
  (`coco_consult_forget_rest`). A read that stops at a syntax error forgets
  nothing more.
- **The re-read is `lb_reread`.** It reads the file and gives the registry
  the new text and time (`coco_module_set_text`). Then it consults the text
  muted, with the module load's own settings: `ownload`, `double_quotes`
  codes, and the collector vouched as for a load. The old text is kept, never
  freed: a load in another thread may be reading it.

WHERE IT DIFFERS FROM swipl:

- **A file with no clauses.** swipl does not count it as loaded
  (`source_file/1` fails for it), so ensure_loaded/1 and `if(not_loaded)`
  read it every time. cocolog holds it as loaded.
- **Order beside asserted clauses** (swipl's since 2.14.1, below). Say the
  program asserts to a predicate the file defines, and the file is then
  read again:
  - swipl puts the new clauses where the old ones stood, before the asserted
    one: `[file2,file3,asserted]`;
  - 2.14.0 appended them: `[asserted,file2,file3]`;
  - a consult did the same through 2.13.

NOT DONE:

- **Across processes.** A predicate's rows that an earlier process's
  consult put in the database stay after a re-read here that no longer
  defines it, if this process has not read that predicate. The drop walks
  only the predicates this process holds.
- **Threads.** A library(thread) thread's store keeps the module as that
  thread loaded it, and a re-read touches only the store that reads. Green
  tasks share their one store.
- **The registry keeps every text it held**, one more per re-read: a stated
  leak.

PROVED:

- **`test/files/reload.pl`** (new) agrees with swipl 9.0.4 over 45 lines.
  After ensure_loaded/1 it checks:
  - ensure_loaded/1 again, and `if(not_loaded)`, `if(changed)` and
    `if(exists)` on an unchanged file: nothing is read;
  - the file replaced by a newer one: ensure_loaded/1 and `if(not_loaded)`
    read nothing, and `if(changed)` reads it, after which the dropped
    predicate raises;
  - an older file: `if(changed)` reads nothing;
  - consult/1: the file is read and the predicate is back;
  - consult/1 again, `[r]` and `if(true)`: each reads, and each clause is
    held once;
  - a consulted file, edited and consulted: its dropped predicate raises;
  - a dynamic predicate keeps the program's assert across a re-read (the
    case sorted the clauses, as the order differed; since 2.14.1 it holds
    the order).
- **`test/files/consult.pl`**: 39 lines, with `[nofile]` raising.
- **`test/reconsult.pl`:**
  - use_module/1 under two spellings, then consult/1: read again and held
    once, `[1,2]-2` with two reads (2.13 gave `[1,2]-1`);
  - the `-s` program that consults itself reads itself again, `[1]-2`;
  - a new section with two processes on `--embed`. The first runs
    use_module/1, asserts to the file's dynamic predicate, swaps the file and
    consults it: `[3]-[asserted]-unknown`. The second loaded nothing; it sees
    the assert and neither version of the module (`unknown-[asserted]-unknown`).
- **`test/repl.pl`**: use_module/1, then `[file].`, then a findall/3 answers

- **`test/solve.cicili`**, at the C seam:

- **An arm per rule, each red:**

  - nothing dropped: reload's `dropped` and `c_dropped`, reconsult's module

  - `if(exists)` always: reload reads twice more;
  - 2.13's toplevel consult: the toplevel check, `L = [1,2,1,2]`;

- **Lesson 00** says it in a section of its own, checks it with two must/3

- **Narrow cases green**, with the server up and no SKIP: the lint case (2

## A file read again puts its clauses where swipl's reload does (2.14.1)

2.14.0 recorded one difference it left (above): a file read again put its
new clauses after everything else in the predicate. So a predicate the
program had asserted into came back `[asserted,file2,file3]`, where swipl
9.0.4 answers `[file2,file3,asserted]`. Now the order is swipl's, in every
case `test/files/reload_order.pl` probes. Each rule below was probed
against swipl.

WHAT IT DOES:

- **A pointer starts at the predicate's first clause, and each clause the
  file says now looks from it for a clause it is a variant of** -- one the
  file put there before, or one the program asserted (no file put it
  there).
  - Found, that clause stays where it stands and the pointer moves past it.
    An asserted one becomes the file's: held once, and gone when the file
    stops saying it (`e_adopted: [1,2,3]`, then `e_dropped: [1,2]`).
  - Not found, the new clause goes in before the pointer: before the first
    clause from the pointer that is still there, or last when none is.
    `[1,2]` with `a` asserted after it, read again as `[3,4]`, is
    `[3,4,a]`; with `z` put in front by asserta/1 it is `[3,4,z]` -- the new
    clauses go before the asserted one wherever it stood.
  - What the file put there and does not say again goes, as through 2.14.0.
- **No candidate is another file's clause, or one the pointer has passed.**
  The program's twin of a clause the file says after it stays, and the
  file's own goes in again (`bp_passed: [z,1,z]`). A clause equal to
  another file's is said again beside it (`mg_other_no_candidate:
  [2,1,2]`).
- **A variant is the same clause whatever its variables are called**
  (`w_variant_kept`), and nothing else: `sh(A, B)` is no variant of
  `sh(Z, Z)` (`sh_shared`), and an atom spelled like a variable's name is no
  variable (`wq_quoted`, `wb_inside_name`).
- **A file read for the first time appends**, beside what the program
  asserted (`q_first_read: [1,a,a,1]`). In a file read AGAIN a predicate new
  to the file is placed too (`nq_new_to_file: [a,b]`), because swipl asks
  per file, not per predicate.
- **A call open on the predicate keeps the clauses that stood when it
  began**, and a call after the read sees the new order (`of_open:
  [1,2,a]`, `of_after: [0,1,2,a]`). A directive half way through the read
  sees the new clauses so far and the asserted one, the old ones out of
  sight (`mid: [3,a]`).
- **Every way a file is read again**: consult/1, `[File]`, load_files/2,
  the toplevel's `[F].` and `consult(F).`, a module's re-read
  (`lb_reread`), and `cocolog run` and `cocolog consult` on a store that
  holds the file. Across processes too: test/reconsult.pl answers
  `[1,2,3,9]` on `--embed` and over the wire, where 2.14.0 answered
  `[9,1,2,3]`.

HOW:

- **The hosts say whether the file was read before** (AGAIN), as swipl
  decides it per file. `coco_library_note_load` answers whether the store
  had noted the file; `lb_load_file` asks `coco_store_loaded` before it
  notes it; a module's re-read is one by definition; `coco_consult_again`
  hands it to the consult. A predicate that holds the file's clauses, of
  the store's mute, is placed whatever AGAIN says (`coco_pred_holds`): a
  second process's table of loads does not know a file the first process
  read, and the rows do.
- **At the file's first clause of a predicate the reload is taken**
  (`coco_reload_begin`, from `coco_reload_for`): O, the clauses the
  predicate holds then, each with its kind -- the file's own, asserted, or
  another's -- and each candidate's shape. Then the file's old clauses go,
  at the first clause, as through 2.14.0 (`coco_pred_forget_from`, which
  keeps the update view). Their cells stay in the store, orphaned, until it
  compacts, so O still names them. A predicate that held nothing but the
  file's own clauses takes no state: each clause goes after the last, which
  is that order.
- **A candidate is found by its shape and told by a walk.**
  - `coco_reload_hash` hashes a term where it lies, on the heap or in the
    store (which lays a compound out as the heap does and shares the
    machine's tables): each functor, atom and integer, a string's bytes, a
    float's bits, a big integer and a rational by value, and a variable as
    a variable.
  - The candidates sit in buckets by shape, each chain ascending, and a
    bucket's head drops for good what the pointer has passed
    (`coco_reload_find`).
  - `coco_reload_variant` walks the new clause on the heap beside the stored
    one, with a variable map both ways (a store variable is keyed from 2^39
    on).
  - Each of the two guards the other: a hash that answers one shape for
    everything, or a walk that compares no atom or integer, leaves every
    case green, and both together turn it red.
- **The new clause is put where it goes** (`coco_reload_insert`).
  - Before the pointer, at a place: `coco_pred_insert_at`, a sixth site that
    moves the clause list and the arrays beside it (keys, origins, muted,
    codes, the deaths). It drops the argument index, as asserta/1 does.
  - Or after the last, as an assertz, the index kept.
  - **Open calls**: `coco_frames_on` takes the place. Act 2 moves on only the
    frames at or past it (asserta/1's is the place 0), and act 3 counts the
    frames an insert there would show the new clause to: one with a clause
    before the place still to try and its end past it. For those, every
    live clause from the place dies where it stands and comes again after
    the new one, a copy each (`coco_reload_relocate`). The open call sees
    what it saw; a new call sees the file's order, and O follows the
    copies.
- **An adopted clause is written again** with its file's name (the
  backend's `on_assert`), so a second process holds it as the file's too.

WHERE IT DIFFERS FROM swipl:

- **A module's file read again adopts no asserted clause.** Its read is
  muted: the module's clauses never reach the knowledge base, while the
  asserted clause's rows did. Its own clause goes in beside it:
  test/solve.cicili's `a,b,a`, where swipl answers `[a,b]`.
- **A directive that asserts at the end of the predicate being read** puts
  its clause before the read's next clauses. swipl puts it after them when
  its pointer still stands on a clause of the file's.
- **A compaction while the read runs** (a directive's four million cells of
  garbage) moves every cell O names. After it, the read's clauses of that
  predicate go after the last.
- **Across processes, only a predicate that holds the file's clauses is
  placed.** A predicate new to the file appends after what the program
  asserted, where in one process it would be placed. swipl has no second
  process to compare.

COST (callgrind, instructions, the start-up included). The binary was
built twice from one emitted C file, with the reload and with it taken
out. The file is 100 dynamic predicates of 50 clauses each, every clause a
body over a compound, a string and a list (5 000 clauses):

| run | with the reload | without | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| read once | 77.08 M | 77.14 M | none: a first read takes no state |
| read twice | 154.86 M | 154.78 M | +0.05 %: the file's own clauses alone take none either |
| read, one clause asserted into each predicate, read again | 182.68 M | 155.71 M | +27.0 M |

- **The third row is the cost.** It is 5 400 instructions for each clause
  read again, where reading one costs 15 600 (the second read, 77.8 M): a
  re-read beside asserted clauses is 35 % dearer than appending was.
- Of the 27.0 M, 15.2 M is the hashes (5 000 new clauses on the heap and 5
  100 candidates in the store, 1 500 each). The rest, inlined into
  `coco_assert_from`, is the walks and the inserts.
- The first cut matched by the text the store writes of a clause: 324.19 M
  on that run, +168.5 M. A hash over a copy of each candidate cost 199.12 M,
  and the hash and walk where each clause lies cost 182.68 M.
- **The untraced engine is untouched** (`tools/flow/zero.sh`, 2.14.0 built
  beside this one from its own commit): the work less its padding is
  65 748 488 against 65 748 331 instructions on nrev, 42 471 541 against
  42 471 692 on queens and 47 813 749 against 47 814 173 on lookup (each
  under 0.001 %), the padding the same to the instruction.

PROVED:

- **`test/files/reload_order.pl`** (new) agrees with swipl 9.0.4 over 43
  lines, a pair of files for each rule above, run by test/files.pl as its
  43rd case:
  - every clause changed, beside clauses asserted before and after;
  - clauses kept, added at the end, added in front, removed, reordered, in
    the middle, duplicated, and variants;
  - a static predicate;
  - the file's clauses split around what the program asserted, read again
    three times;
  - the pointer on a clause the program put in front;
  - what a directive half way through the read sees;
  - adoption, and what the pointer passed;
  - a predicate new to a file read again;
  - a first read;
  - two files of one predicate;
  - a call open on the predicate while its file is read again.
- **`test/files/reload.pl`**: its last check sorted the clauses of a
  module's dynamic predicate, as the order differed, and now holds
  swipl's (`[file2, asserted]`).
- **`test/reconsult.pl`**: the edited file's clauses before the asserted
  one, `[1,2,3,9]`, across two processes on `--embed` and over the wire
  (2.14.0's `[9,1,2,3]`).
- **`test/solve.cicili`**, at the C seam:
  - read again: `3,1,a`;
  - a first read appends beside an asserted twin, `a,a,b`, and read again
    the twin is the file's, held once, `a,b`;
  - a muted read again adopts nothing, `a,b,a`.
- **An arm per rule**, each built from the emitted C with one rule taken
  out and run through the case. Sixteen are red:
  - no reload (2.14.0's order): 33 of the 43 lines;
  - no adoption: `e_adopted`, `e_dropped`, `e2_held_once`,
    `ba_taken_passed`, `nq_new_to_file`;
  - a first read placed as a re-read: `fq`, `fr`, `q` (both), `mf_both`
    and the two `mg` lines;
  - AGAIN ignored, and the hosts passing 0, alike: `k_after`, `nq` and
    `nr`;
  - another file's clause a candidate: `mg_other_no_candidate`;
  - a clause the pointer passed a candidate: `bp_passed`,
    `ba_taken_passed`;
  - the pointer left on the file's own clause: `w_variant_kept`,
    `s8_mixed`, the three `sp` lines and `bp_passed`; and on an adopted
    one: `ba_taken_passed`;
  - variables compared as cells, and variables hashed by their cells:
    `w_variant_kept`; the map one way only: `sh_shared`;
  - no relocation for an open call: `of_open: [1,2,0]`; O not following
    the copies: `of_after: [0,a,1,2]`; act 2 moving every frame:
    `of_open: [1,0]`;
  - the hash a constant and the walk comparing no atom or integer: eight
    lines (`s2`, `s10`, `wq`, `wb`, two of `sp`, `ba`, `q_read_again`).

  Two are green, and each guards the other: the hash a constant alone,
  and the walk comparing no atom or integer alone.
- **Narrow cases green**, with the server up and no SKIP: files (all 43

## The green world's size, asked: async_workers/1 (2.15.0)

A program that sized its green work by the world worked the world's rule
out again. library(httpd)'s green pool read COCOLOG_GREEN_WORKERS and
os_cpus/1 itself, and took 4 without library(os) where the world takes the
cores, with no ceiling where the world's is 256. Lesson 54's quantum check
and test/async.pl's took the world to have eight workers: the eighth of
eight children shares the main's worker only where the size divides eight,
and on GitHub's three-core Mac it ran apart from the main and could finish
first (run 41030811820, red at the lesson; 887a472 started one child a
worker and worked the size out as the world does). 2.15.0 asks the world.

WHAT IT DOES:

- **`async_workers(-N)`**, library(async), tier 1 and so a global name.
  Outside a world, N is the workers the next async_run/1 would start, by
  the world's own rule (`coco_g_nworkers`): COCOLOG_GREEN_WORKERS if it
  gives a positive count, else the cores online, 256 at most. Inside a
  world, N is the world's own count, read through the thread-local
  `green_now` on every worker's thread, whatever the variable says by
  then: a world of 2 that sets the variable to 5 answers 2 inside, and 5
  once it has ended. `async_workers(foo)` fails.
- **It is a journal portal by name** (`green:$async_workers/1` in
  `coco_jr_named`, beside getenv/2): it reads the environment and the
  cores, as getenv/2 and os_cpus/1 do, so a replay answers it from its
  entry whatever the environment says by then.
- **library(httpd)'s green mode asks it**; `httpd_world_workers/1` is gone.
  The thread mode still sizes its pool from the cores.
- **Lesson 54 and test/async.pl ask it inside the world** for the quantum
  check (one child a worker, the last on worker 0), and the lesson shows
  the answer inside a world is the one outside said it would start.

PROVED:

- test/async.pl, a new section, "the world's size: async_workers/1": seven
  checks, two in the process and five in child processes with the
  variable at 2, 300, unset, 0 and `abc` (the last two are no count: the
  cores, as unset).
- test/journal.pl, a new section: a recorded window holds one entry, the
  green module's exit, and its replay with the variable changed answers
  the recorded count.
- Three arms, one rule out each, each red: the outside answer by the
  world's rule (the cores alone: `=2`, `=300` and unset red), the inside
  answer the world's own (the rule's instead: the same three red, through
  the answer after the world sets the variable, `2-2-5-5` for `2-2-2-5`),
  and the journal entry (none: both of journal's new checks red, the
  journal empty and the replay answering the box's 1 where 4 was
  recorded). Lesson 54 stays green under the second arm, as it should: no
  world of its own sets the variable.
- Alone and green: test/async.pl, test/journal.pl, test/httpd.pl (its
  green pool), test/flowchart.pl (the rebuilt tables carry
  `flow_t_c('$async_workers',1,...)`, `flow_t_lib(async_workers,1,...)`
  and its signature `[-]`), the lint case and lesson 54.
- tools/flow/zero.sh against 2.14.1: nrev +665 instructions of 70.9
  million, queens +84, lookup -485, the padding the same.

The full local `make test` was not run; CI runs the suite.

## The folds evaluate, and term_to_atom/2 reads (2.15.1)

The token benchmark (bench/tokens.pl, 273585f) is SWI-Prolog as a model
writes it, and building it ran into three places where cocolog answered
otherwise than swipl: an aggregate over an expression
(`aggregate_all(sum(I+W+R+O), ...)` raised), `term_to_atom/2` with both
arguments bound (it failed), and print_message/2 (it does not exist). The
harness was written round all three. 2.15.1 takes the first two away, and
the card row that told the model something false.

WHAT IT DOES:

- **sum_list/2, max_list/2 and min_list/2 evaluate their elements**
  (lib/lists.cicili), as SWI's own clauses do: `Sum1 is Sum0 + X`, and
  `Max1 is max(H, Max0)` after the first element taken as it is. A plain
  number still goes through the C loop (`coco_l_sum`, `coco_l_extreme`),
  and the first element that is none -- an expression, a rational, `pi`
  -- turns the fold into SWI's: the sum so far a cell, and each step
  is/2's own `+`, `max` or `min` over the two (`coco_l_eval2`). So an atom
  raises is/2's `type_error(evaluable, a/0)` and an unbound element its
  instantiation_error (2.15.0: `type_error(evaluable, a)` and
  `type_error(evaluable, _G704)`), and a lone first element is never
  evaluated: `max_list([1+1], M)` is `1+1`, `max_list([a], M)` is `a`.
- **aggregate_all/3's sum, max and min evaluate too**
  (lib/builtins.cicili): `sum(X)` is `S is S0 + X` from 0, and `max(X)`
  and `min(X)` are `M is max(M0, X)` from the first solution's
  `max(X, X)`, so a lone atom raises where 2.15.0 answered `a`. The
  witness forms, `max(X, W)` and `min(X, W)`, take the first solution only
  if it is a number (`type_error(number, X)` otherwise; 2.15.0 took `a`)
  and a later one only if it compares greater or less (`X > Max0`, which
  evaluates, and which a NaN never passes), keeping it as it was given:
  `max(2+3, b)`. Through 2.15.0 an expression or a rational raised
  `type_error(number, ...)` in all five forms, and an atom alone was a
  max.
- **term_to_atom/2 reads its text whenever the text is bound**, whatever
  the term: `term_to_atom(answer(K, E), 'answer(cost,24.0)')` binds K and
  E, and `term_to_atom(f(a), 'f( a )')` holds. 2.15.0 wrote a bound term
  and compared the two texts, so both failed, and with both arguments
  unbound it raised `type_error(text, _)` where swipl writes the variable;
  it writes it now.
- **Card row A1 is gone** (tools/cocolint/traps.jsonl, 30 rows). It said
  that `atan/2`, `atan2/2`, `copysign/2`, `random/1`, `random_float`, the
  hyperbolic functions, `lgamma/1`, `erf/1`, `erfc/1`, `lsb/1`,
  `popcount/1`, `getbit/2`, `powm/3`, `nexttoward/2`, `cputime` and
  `rational/1` are not evaluable, and every one has been since 2.5.0 (only
  `log/2` is missing, and swipl 9.0.4 lacks it too): the card arm of the
  benchmark would have paid for a workaround to nothing. Lesson 37 counts
  30 and its history says why; the selftest's comment and GUIDE.md follow,
  and the cites of W2, X2, T2, H1 and F1 moved with the edits to

## print_message/2 and sumlist/2 (2.16.0)

The token benchmark found both missing (bench/tokens/README.md): a program
written for swipl that reports with `print_message/2` raised an existence
error here, and `sumlist/2`, the old name swipl still autoloads for
`sum_list/2` from library(backcomp), was unknown. Both are there now, held
to swipl 9.0.4, with what print_message/2 stands on.

- **library(print_message)** (`library/print_message.pl`), TIER 1:
  preloaded at start-up as library(async) is, since swipl has these with no
  library to load. print_message/2, message_to_string/2,
  print_message_lines/3, and the message_hook/3, prolog:message//1 and
  prolog:error_message//1 a program defines. The kinds and their prefixes
  (`ERROR: `, `Warning: `, `% ` for informational and information, none for
  the rest; silent prints nothing; a query to user_output, the rest to
  user_error), every prefix again after each `nl`, the elements of a line
  (Format-Args, nl, at_same_line, flush, full_stop, ansi/3, url/1,2,
  begin/end), the location line a directive's error or warning carries, the
  text of every ISO and SWI error term (boot/messages.pl's words, its BSD-2
  terms in the file's header), `Unknown message: T`, a message that comes
  round again said once (`Recursive warning message: T`), and the lines
  flushed when they end, as swipl's.
- **message_hook/3 sees every kind**, silent too, as swipl's
  print_message_guarded does; only the system's printing honours silent and
  verbose.
- **The flag verbose** (`normal`; set_prolog_flag/2 takes any atom, the
  process's): under `silent`, swipl -q's, informational and banner print
  nothing.
- **source_location/2** answers the file (its real path) and the line of
  the directive whose goal is running, and fails elsewhere, as swipl's
  (`sloc_file`/`sloc_line`, appended to the machine, set around the goal by
  the load and put back after it).
- **`~N` in format/1,2,3**: a newline only where a line is open. The engine
  keeps whether one is open on stdout and on stderr -- ONE column for the
  two, as swipl's user_output and user_error share one -- from what it
  writes itself (`coco_out_note`, `coco_out_puts`, `coco_out_putc` in
  lib/term.cicili: write/1 and its kin, nl/0, tab/1, format, listing, the
  reports); a capture has its own column from 0; a term sink starts at 0;
  library(stream)'s files answer for themselves (`st_open`, through the new
  `coco_m_sink_open_install` hook, in lib/sdk.cicili for an out-of-tree
  module with `coco_m_out_note`/`coco_m_out_open`).
- **The engine's reports begin a line of their own**, as swipl's do, being
  print_message/2's: a directive's Warning and ERROR, an initialization
  goal's, the goal's own uncaught ERROR and a syntax error that ends a
  consult (`coco_load_message`, `coco_load_note`, `lb_say_text`,
  cocolog.cicili). Through 2.15.2 `half` and the report's tag shared a line.
- **A qualified grammar rule keeps its qualifier**: `M:H --> B` is
  `M:H2 :- B2` (lib/dcg.cicili, `coco_dcg_requalify`); through 2.15.2 the
  qualifier took the two arguments, a `:'/4 nobody calls. Whether there is
  one is a flag: the first cut tested `mod != 0`, and under `cocolog run`
  -- a fresh machine, whose consult reads each clause from heap cell 0 --
  the module's atom IS cell 0, so every prolog:message//1 rule lost its
  qualifier there alone. The two hooks are stored as `'$prolog_message'/3`
  and `'$prolog_error_message'/3` (lib/kb.cicili, `coco_hook_head`), apart
  from a program's own message/3.
- **A format written `"..."` is its text**: a code list here (the flag
  double_quotes is `codes`) where swipl's is a string. print_message/2
  hands either to format/3 as it is; message_to_string/2, which joins the
  formats as atoms, and message_lines/1, whose elements are written with
  `~w`, take the list's atom (`'$pm_text'`, `'$pm_line_text'`). Before that
  `message_to_string(format("a~w", [1]), S)` answered `"[97,126,119]"`.
- **sumlist/2** is library(backcomp)'s one clause, `sumlist(L, S) :-
  sum_list(L, S)` (lib/lists.cicili), so it evaluates as sum_list/2 does.

The cocolint index lists library(print_message) as tier 1 (`ix_preloaded`)

## atom_length/2 and string_length/2 raise swipl's errors (2.16.1)

Through 2.16.0 atom_length/2 wrote whatever it was given, counted the
writing, and unified the count with its second argument. So a length that
was no integer failed where swipl 9.0.4 raises type_error(integer, L)
(`atom_length(abc, foo)`, `atom_length(abc, 3.0)`), a compound was the
length of its writing (`atom_length(f(x), N)` was 4, swipl's
type_error(text, f(x))), and so was a list (`atom_length([a,b], N)` was 5,
swipl's 2; `atom_length([a|_], N)` counted the variable's name too, 7 for
`[a|_G1]` in a query, swipl's instantiation_error).
string_length/2 failed on the length in the same way, wrote a compound, and
took a list that mixed codes and characters for text.

- Both read their text as swipl's PL_get_text does with CVT_ALL
  (`coco_len_text`, lib/solve.cicili). An atom, a number or a string is the
  text the writer writes unquoted, and a compound that is no list is
  type_error(text, T). A list is codes when its first element is an
  integer and characters when that element is a character, and every
  element after it is held to that kind (`coco_len_list`):
  type_error(character_code, X) for a code (0 to U+10FFFF) and for a first
  element that is neither, type_error(character, X) for a character, and
  instantiation_error for an unbound element. Its tail is held to `[]`: an
  unbound tail is instantiation_error, and anything else is
  type_error(text, L), a list that is its own tail included. A list is as
  long as it has elements, in either unit; under `text_units = bytes` a
  character is an atom of one byte, as atom_chars/2 has it there.
- The length (`coco_len_answer`): unbound, it takes the count; an
  integer of either kind is compared, so a negative or a boxed one fails,
  as swipl's does; anything else is type_error(integer, L). The text is
  asked first, so `atom_length(f(x), foo)` is the text's error and
  `atom_length([a|_], foo)` instantiation_error, as in swipl.
- `[]` is an atom here, two characters long: cocolog does not tell `[]`
  from `'[]'`, and the atom is what `format(atom(A), '~w', [[]])` and
  `atom_codes(A, "[]")` make. swipl's `[]` is the empty list, so its
  `atom_length([], N)` is 0, while its `atom_length('[]', N)` is 2.
  string_length/2 keeps `[]` as the empty list, as it was through 2.16.0
  (under `double_quotes = codes`, a "" is `[]`).
- The predicates whose clauses asked a length first (lib/builtins.cicili)
  ask `'$atom_text_length'/3` or `'$string_text_length'/3` instead: the
  same reading, but anything that is no text is that predicate's own
  error, of the whole term, as swipl's are. That is `atom` for sub_atom/5,
  `atomic` for atom_concat/3 and string_concat/3 in mode (-,-,+), and
  `string` for sub_string/5. sub_atom/5 had swipl's type_error(atom, T)
  from `'$atom_byte_length'/2`, after its call of atom_length/2, which the
  new reading would have taken first: `sub_atom(f(x), 0, 1, _, _)`
  became type_error(text, f(x)), and a partial list instantiation_error,
  until these helpers. The three others took a compound's writing for its
  text through 2.16.0 (`atom_concat(X, Y, f(x))` gave five splits of
  `f(x)`) and raise swipl's error now. A list that is text stays text to
  them all, as it was: under codes, a program's "abc" is one, and swipl's
  is a string. One goal replaces one goal in each clause, so the
  inference counts are the same. 200 rounds of sub_atom/5, atom_concat/3,
  sub_string/5 and string_concat/3 count 121 602 on 2.16.0 and on 2.16.1.
- A cyclic list or compound given to either length predicate is
  type_error(text, T), as swipl's. Through 2.16.0 it was the length of its
  factors' writing (`@(S_1,[S_1=f(S_1)])`, 19), which test/cyclic.pl had
  pinned since 1.10.18 fixed the crash.

PROVED:
- test/files/atom_length.pl (new, the 48th case): 96 lines identical to

NOT swipl's:
- An error from either predicate carries cocolog's context, unbound, as
  every core builtin's does, where swipl's is `context(system:
  atom_length/2, _)`, so print_message/2 writes no `atom_length/2: `

## Errors name the predicate, `[]` is no atom, and text is read as swipl reads it (3.0.0, reasoning 1.0.27)

The four differences from swipl 9.0.4 that 2.16.1 stated (under NOT swipl's,
above) are closed: an error's context, `atom_length([], N)`, the four
callers given a list, and the other text builtins taking a compound or a
list that mixes codes and characters. The work found more of the same kind
and fixed it in the same release. It is a MAJOR: a program that worked can
stop working.

What stops working:
- `[]` is not `'[]'`. `atom([])` fails and `atomic([])` holds,
  `callable([])` fails, `[] == '[]'` fails, `atom_length([], N)` is 0, and
  `atom_codes(A, "[]")` makes the atom `'[]'`, which is not `[]`. A program
  that tested the list's end with atom/1, or built `'[]'` from text and
  compared it with `[]`, now takes the other branch.
- TEXT THAT 2.x WROTE READS BACK OTHERWISE (cicilang's finding, on
  3.16.0): 2.x wrote the atom `'[]'` as `[]`, the two being one atom then,
  so a term it wrote as text with `'[]'` in it -- a cache of clauses
  written by writeq/1, say -- reads back under 3.x with the list's end
  where the atom stood, and nothing says so. cicilang's per-header
  summaries of libc++ 18 held `operator([])` 5 666 times in 440 files,
  each one the empty list as 3.x read it: the subscript operator lost.
  Drop such text and write it again. An `--embed` store written by 2.x
  asks the same question, and is not tested.
- A compound given as text raises `type_error` (split_string/4,
  string_chars/2, atom_string/2, upcase_atom/2, term_to_atom/2's text and
  the rest), where through 2.16 its writing was the text. A list that mixes
  codes and characters raises `type_error(character, C)` or its kin.
- sub_atom/5, sub_string/5, atom_concat/3 and string_concat/3 refuse a list
  (`type_error(atom, L)`, `type_error(string, L)`, `type_error(atomic, L)`).
  Under the default `double_quotes = codes` a `"..."` is a list, so
  `sub_string(S, 0, 1, _, "#")` raises. Write `'#'`.
- An unbound culprit of a type error is `instantiation_error`
  (`nb_getval(_, V)`, `getenv(_, V)`, `statistics(_, V)`, `sort(_, L)`,
  `tab(_)`), where it was `type_error(atom, _)` and the like.
- Builtins that failed now raise: `length(a, N)` and `memberchk(a, b)`
  raise `type_error(list, _)`, and `char_code(_, 0xD800)` raises
  `type_error(character_code, 55296)`. Builtins that raised another error
  than swipl's now raise swipl's: format/2,3 (`~d` of `a` is
  `type_error(evaluable, a/0)`), between/3, succ/2, plus/3, op/3,
  current_op/3, halt/1, tab/1, `=..`, compare/3, the flags, nth0/3 and
  nth1/3, sort/4, keysort/2, with_output_to/2, write_term/2's options, the
  file and environment builtins' text, numlist/3, list_to_set/2,
  compound_name_arity/3 and compound_name_arguments/3, retractall/1,
  file_base_name/2 and file_directory_name/2.
- An error's second argument is `context(system:Name/Arity, _)`, where it
  was unbound. A message nothing caught begins `Name/Arity: `, as does what
  print_message/2 writes for such a ball: `ERROR: -s main: atom_length/2:
  Arguments are not sufficiently instantiated`.

What changed (each held to swipl 9.0.4):
- THE CONTEXT. A core builtin, and a row of a compiled-in module, raises
  with swipl's context, from a row of `*error-contexts*` (`coco_err_ctx`).
  A C builtin is named by its own indicator. A library predicate is named
  by the frame swipl's own raise names: memberchk/2 by `'$memberchk'/3`,
  length/2 bare (`context(length/2, _)`), findall/3's goal by
  `'$bags':findall_loop/4`, forall/2's by `'$apply':forall/2`, and
  char_type/2 and code_type/2 by a bare `char_type/2` for an unbound
  character. A goal the step loop meets that is no goal is
  `'<meta-call>'/1`'s error, and call/N's own for its closure. once/1,
  ignore/1, not/1 and catch/3 called as terms raise their own error for an
  argument that is no goal (`coco_construct_bad`), and `throw(_)` is
  throw/1's `instantiation_error`. An unknown procedure in a search's own
  goal term names its caller, as swipl's does. The uncaught error's text
  and print_message/2 write the `Name/Arity: ` prefix from the context
  (`coco_err_caller`; library(print_message)'s `'$pm_caller'`), and the
  type error's ` (a compound)`, ` (an atom)` after the culprit.
- `[]` AND `'[]'` (swipl 7). Two entries of the atom table: `[]`, the
  list's end (`coco_nil_id`, asked with `coco_is_nil`), and `'[]'`, an atom
  of two characters (`coco_intern_tnil`), which the writer quotes. A text
  read from `[]` is the empty list, so `atom_length([], N)` is 0, and
  `atom_length('[]', N)` is 2.
- TEXT AS swipl's PL_get_text READS IT (`coco_tx_get` and its `CVT_*`
  flags). Each text builtin takes what swipl's takes and refuses the rest
  with swipl's error: a compound is `type_error(T, C)`, a list is held to
  its first element's kind (codes or characters), a partial list is
  `instantiation_error`. A predicate whose text may be unbound fails there
  where swipl's does (`CVT_VARNOFAIL`, `coco_tx_varnofail`).
  sub_atom/5, atom_concat/3, string_concat/3 and sub_string/5 read
  `CVT_ATOMIC` alone, so a list is no text to them.
- MORE OF THE SAME. Arithmetic over a list of one element or a string of
  one character evaluates to its code (`X is "a" + 0` is 97), and `[]` is
  `type_error(evaluable, [])`. An evaluable function's error names the
  function, `X is foo(1, 2, a)` naming `a/0`. memberchk/2 binds an open
  list's tail, as swipl's does. format/2,3's `~d`, `~e`, `~f`, `~g` and
  `~r` evaluate their argument. A syntax error's reason is swipl's
  sentence.
- between/3 AND numlist/3 CHECK AS swipl's DO, ONCE A CALL. between/3's
  three arguments are checked by `'$between'/4` (L an integer, H one or
  `inf` or `infinite`, X an integer or unbound), where through 2.16 a
  bound X that was no integer failed, L and H were compared as any
  numbers, and `between(1, inf, a)` ran for ever. The answers come from
  `'$between_up'/3`, which checks nothing. The first cut asked
  `'$between'/4` in between/3's first clause, which the recursion
  re-entered, so every answer paid a failing C call and a backtrack where
  2.16's integer(X) guard had failed inside the clause's entry. Five runs
  of `forall(between(1, 3000000, _), true)` took 1.10 to 1.22 s of user
  time against 2.16.1's 0.65 to 0.93. test/window.pl found it: its retry
  counts doubled (40 001 retries where 20 001 are). numlist/3 is one
  clause over `'$numlist'/3`, which checks L and H as swipl's
  must_be(integer, X) does and fails for L > H. Its first cut asked a C
  helper in the first clause and cost every call a backtrack. Now
  between/3's enumeration takes 0.61 s against 2.16.1's 0.68 s (medians
  of five), and `forall(between(1, 300000, _), numlist(1, 3, _))` 0.11 s
  against 0.14 s. An answer of between/3 is one inference fewer (20 000
  answers 100 004 against 120 001), a bound X one more (the check swipl
  makes), and numlist/3 one fewer a call.
- `name/2` was written as a builtin and taken out again. As a C builtin it
  shadows a program's own name//0 (`test/files/dcg.pl`), so it waits on
  swipl's rule for redefining a system predicate, and stays among the
  predicates that are not there (COMPAT.md).

The libraries (reasoning 1.0.27; 1.0.26 is already spent, on the

## last/2 enumerates a partial list, as swipl's does (3.0.1)

`last(L, X)` with `L` unbound, and with a partial list such as `[a|T]`,
failed: the C row of 1.12.2 answered a proper list in one step and every
other list with a failure (3.0.0's NOT swipl's, above, and COMPAT.md).
swipl 9.0.4 enumerates there, by library(lists)'s

    last([X|Xs], Last) :- last_(Xs, X, Last).
    last_([], Last, Last).
    last_([X|Xs], _, Last) :- last_(Xs, X, Last).

-- `L = [X]`, then `L = [_A, X]`, and on, and for `[a|T]` `T = []` with
`X = a`, then `T = [X]`, and on: the shortest list first, Last always the
element at its end. cocolog answers the same now, answer by answer.

- THE ROW DECLINES A PARTIAL LIST (`:declines`, `coco_m_decline`), an
  unbound List among them, to the Coco half's last/2, swipl's clauses over
  `'$last_gen'/3`, which nothing else reaches -- as length/2, nth0/3,
  nth1/3 and reverse/2 decline theirs since 1.12.2. The row asks once and
  the helper the recursion comes back to tests nothing (between/3's
  `'$between_up'/3`), so each answer after the first is one step.
- A PROPER LIST IS STILL ONE STEP, and now one walk: `coco_l_last` keeps the
  last cell it passes, where 3.0.0 walked the list twice
  (`coco_m_list_length`, then `coco_l_step` to its end). statistics/2 says 3
  for `last([a,b,c], _)` with the call/1 and the statistics/2 that measure
  it, what `atom(a)` costs, on the 3.0.0 binary and on this one alike, and
  the same for a list of 1000; `last(_, _)` is 4 here (the clause and its
  helper) and `last([a,b|_], z)` 6.
- WHAT FAILED STILL FAILS: the empty list, an atom, `'[]'`, `[a|foo]`,
  `[a,b|c]`, a compound and a number, where swipl's head fails too and
  nothing raises; and a list that is its own tail, which swipl's clause
  walks for ever -- the one difference left.
- `'$last'/2` IS GONE: the old walk's second name, which nothing had called
  since 1.12.2 took last/2's clause away, and which could not share the new
  function (a declining row's function takes FOUND).
- THE TREE'S OWN CALLERS GAVE IT NO PARTIAL LIST. The tree's Prolog calls
  last/2 205 times, 169 of them in library/reasoning/translate.pl, every one
  written against a last/2 that failed for a partial list, so any that
  relied on the failure would now enumerate. A throwaway build whose
  declined path wrote each call it declined to a file ran the cases
  translate, reason, normalise, flowchart, flowdebug, lint and tokens and
  lessons 01, 31, 42, 43, 44, 46 and 51 of tutorials/library: every one
  green, or `done`, and not one call declined.

Held by:
- test/files/last.pl, the 51st case: a proper list, no list, an unbound
  list and partial ones (`[a|T]`, `[a, b|T]`, with Last bound, Last the
  list's head, a variable the list shares), the first answers of each in
  order, each answer printed as it comes, backtracking into the
  enumeration past a failed test, and the first six lengths counted. 38

- test/files/error_context.pl: `last(_, _)`, which 3.0.0's case left out

- test/engine.pl's one-step section: a new check, last/2 of an unbound

## A loadable module's errors name the module (3.0.2)

3.0.0 stated, under NOT swipl's (above), that "a loadable module's own
predicate raises with the context unbound ... Its message then has no
`Name/Arity: ` prefix." It names its module now, as swipl 9.0.4 names a
foreign predicate's errors. A patch: a program that matches
`error(Formal, _)` reads what it read, and what is new is a context bound
where it was unbound and a prefix before a message.

WHAT swipl DOES, probed: a foreign predicate's error carries the module that
defines it, whatever its library is called -- library(socket)'s
`tcp_socket(a)` raises `error(uninstantiation_error(a),
context(socket:tcp_socket/1, _))`, process_kill/1's foreign half names
`process:process_kill/2`, library(sha)'s sha_hash/3 `crypto_hash:sha_hash/3`,
md5_hash/3 `md5:md5_hash/3`, read_line_to_codes/2
`read_util:read_line_to_codes/2` -- and print_message/2 writes `M:N/A: `
before the message unless M is user, system or a `$` one (messages.pl's
caller//1), as `coco_err_caller` and library(print_message)'s
`'$pm_caller'` already did. A foreign helper that raises names itself:
on_signal/3's `system:'$on_signal'/4`.

What changed:
- THE SEAM SAYS WHICH MODULE IT CALLS: `kmod` on the engine (appended), the
  module's index in the registry plus one, set before each dispatcher call
  -- in `coco_module_call` (the walk an atom goal, and a goal after a
  decline, takes), `coco_module_call_resolving` (a compound goal's first
  call) and `coco_module_call_at` (every call after, by the functor's
  remembered owner) -- and cleared by the step when the module's call
  returns (lib/solve-loop.cicili), so it is 0 outside one. Not put back by
  the seam: putting it back after the call made `coco_module_call_at`'s
  tail call a call with a frame, 11 instructions a module call (365 against
  354 on 3.0.0's binary), where the store in the step costs none (below).
- THE LOADER MARKS WHAT A `.so` REGISTERED: `foreign` on the registry's
  entry (appended), set by `lb_load_so` for every module the entry
  registered (`coco_module_set_foreign`, from the registry's count before
  the entry ran).
- `coco_m_raise`, when no row of `*error-contexts*` names the goal in flight
  and a foreign module answers it, raises `context(Module:Name/Arity, _)`:
  the name the module registered, and the C predicate that raised -- a `$`
  helper too, as swipl names its own (`coco_m_module_ctx`, cold). A module
  compiled into the binary (lists, files, builtins ...) keeps 3.0.0's: what
  its rows name, and the rest unbound, as swipl's library predicates written
  over must_be/2 leave it (nth0/3).
- A ROW WINS: library(thread)'s mutex_lock/1, mutex_unlock/1,
  mutex_trylock/1, mutex_destroy/1 and thread_detach/1 are swipl's builtins,
  named `system:Name/Arity` as swipl names them, and mutex_create/1 bare, as
  swipl's PL_error() names it -- six rows, read off swipl 9.0.4.
- NO SDK CHANGE: no new function and the ABI is 1, as it was, so no module
  is rebuilt: the `.so` files `make modules` built from the tree before the
  change ran unchanged under it.

What a program sees: after `use_module(library(sha))`,
`catch(sha_hash(foo, abc, _), error(E, C), true)` binds C to
`context(sha:sha_hash/3, _)`, and uncaught under `-s` it prints ``ERROR:
-s main: sha:sha_hash/3: Domain error: `sha_algorithm' expected, found
`foo'``; `mutex_lock(_)` prints `mutex_lock/1: Arguments are not
sufficiently instantiated`, swipl's text.
